speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister what will be his attitude to the suggested conference of commonwealth prime ministers, which I understand is being placed before the various prime ministers by the new Prime Minister of Great Britain. Does he at this time consider, having regard to the possibility of the United Kingdom entering into a free trade arrangement with Europe, that at the same time something in the nature of a British commonwealth trade conference would be acceptable and indeed needful?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman repeat the last words of his question?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister not consider that in view of the possible adherence by the United Kingdom to a European free trade agreement, at this time something in the nature of a commonwealth trade conference in so far as Canada is concerned is not only requisite but needful?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext:
These conferences have always been very useful. We have had no information other than newspaper reports of any consideration being given at this time to an attempt to arrange a conference. Of course at this time it would be somewhat inconvenient. I have some legislative proposals that I hope to be able to submit to parliament, and I also hope to be able to be here when they are being discussed in parliament.
I can assure the hon. gentleman that, if there is a suggestion for a conference of representatives of the governments of the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries, the matter will be given very serious and careful consideration, because we do realize, as I think most Canadians do, the value of these exchanges of views and of the need to arrive at decisions which, of course, each government has to arrive at 82715-214
on its own responsibility, but which do all tend to the achievement of the same objective.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext:
Perhaps the Prime
Minister will also answer the other question: whether having regard to these economic developments in Europe he would give consideration to convening a commonwealth trade conference in order to assure and maintain Canada's trade.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, at this time we would not consider that we should attempt to convene a conference on trade until we have further information as to what exactly are the problems the new government in the United Kingdom would consider as having top priority in discussion with the representatives of other commonwealth governments.

subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister supplementary to the questions asked by my leader. In view of the fact that there is an indication that the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom might desire a meeting of the commonwealth prime ministers and that he may also be going to Washington, would the Prime Minister consider requesting the convening of such a meeting of commonwealth prime ministers in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government would not consider at this moment substituting this action for what may be felt by the new Prime Minister of the United Kingdom to be the most urgent action that he should take. The government of Canada will co-operate wholeheartedly with the government of the United Kingdom in trying to arrange anything that may be felt there to be the most urgent matters that require to be dealt with.

subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the statements made by both the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, does the Prime Minister not think this country might take the initiative at this time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS ON TRADE AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister does not feel that this country should take the initiative

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PLANS FOR DEVELOPMENT OF ALBERTA TAR SANDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Trade and Commerce, make a statement to the house concerning the reports that the new Prime Minister of Great Britain has under consideration what is described as a dramatic plan for the development of the Alberta tar sands? I think reports indicate that copies of this plan, which is under study, have been submitted to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This would appear to be a very far-reaching development, and it would be of interest to the house and the country if either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Trade and Commerce would explain just what is under way.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PLANS FOR DEVELOPMENT OF ALBERTA TAR SANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so far as I am
aware the only communication we have had on the subject came from Mr. Carol Wilson, who was formerly general manager of the atomic energy commission of the United States and is now the president of a private firm. He wrote about a plan for developing the tar sands to meet the present oil shortage in Europe. There was nothing new in the letter that I could find, other than suggesting immediate development. He said he sent a copy to the then British ambassador in Washington. I answered the letter and said we were watching with interest the tar sands situation, but we felt that at the moment it is not a development that was justified by present prices for the product. We regard it as more in the nature of a reserve for the future. That is all I have heard on the subject. We have nothing whatever from the British government. As to whether that government is interested or not I have no information.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: REPORTED CEILING ON EXPORTS OF MANUFACTURED COTTON GOODS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED CEILING ON EXPORTS OF MANUFACTURED COTTON GOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Can the


minister comment on the news report that Japan is going to place more ceilings on the export of manufactured cotton goods to Canada? What is the purpose of such action? Is such action not likely to adversely affect the sale of Canadian goods to Japan?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED CEILING ON EXPORTS OF MANUFACTURED COTTON GOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the export of textiles from Japan to Canada is a matter that was discussed when I visited Japan a few months ago. The Japanese have about 5 per cent of our market for textiles, and we think it would be difficult for us to live with a larger proportion.
The ceiling that has been put on in Japan has been put on by the industry, and not at the request of the Canadian government. I think the action taken may have been in furtherance of the thought I left there that Japan should be willing to see their market for textiles in Canada grow gradually with the growth of the total market, rather than flood this country with textiles at any one time. That is all I can say about it. We have had no communication on the subject from Japan. I read the same article to which the hon. member is referring this morning, and that is really all I know about the situation.

maintopic: REPORTED CEILING ON EXPORTS OF MANUFACTURED COTTON GOODS
speechtext: I wonder if I might ask a further supplementary question. Does the minister know whether any action will be taken subsequently to increase the ceilings, or are they placed on for an indefinite period?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED CEILING ON EXPORTS OF MANUFACTURED COTTON GOODS
speechtext: Well, the ceilings were placed, not at the request of anyone here but rather because the industry in Japan thought that was the sound way to develop a continuing market in Canada. As far as purchases of wheat and barley by Japan are concerned, although I do not know whether or not my visit had anything to do with it, since the time of my visit exports of both grains have increased very considerably; in fact, we have a larger proportion of total Japanese imports of those two grains than we have ever had at any time.

The second question reads:
Has consideration been given to any extension of the date of repayment of the $80 million loan to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines beyond April 1, 1957?
The answer is no.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES-INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT STATUS

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES-INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT STATUS
speechtext:
It has no meaning except that Trans-Canada is not at this time making plans to build the pipe line south from Winnipeg to Emerson.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that there was adopted this morning, and it has been approved by His Excellency the Governor General, an order in council setting up a royal commission to deal with the matters that it was agreed would be referred to a royal commission in connection with the dispute between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the union of locomotive firemen and enginemen. I have not yet had certified copies, but as soon as the material work can be done copies will be transmitted to the Clerk of the house for tabling. Perhaps in view of the general interest in this matter hon. members would

like me to read the text of the order in council into the record. If that is desired I would be prepared to do so at once.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
speechtext:
It reads as follows:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report from the Prime Minister stating that in order to provide for settlement of the dispute between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen, which gave rise to a cessation of operations on the railway in January, 1957, it is desirable to appoint a commission under part I of the Inquiries Act to inquire into and report upon the unresolved issues in the dispute.
The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, advise:
1.	That:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Roy Lindsay Kellock, puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Canada,
The Honourable Mr. Justice Campbell C. Mc-Laurin, chief justice of the trial division of the supreme court of Alberta, and
The Honourable Mr. Justice Jean Martineau, puisne judge of the court of Queen's bench for Quebec
be appointed commissioners under part I of the Inquiries Act to inquire into and report upon all matters they deem necessary in order to answer, and to answer the following questions:
(a)	Are firemen (or firemen helpers) required on diesel locomotives in freight and yard service of the Canadian Pacific Railway, including the eastern, prairie and Pacific regions and the Quebec Central and Dominion Atlantic railways?
(b)	If not, what terms and conditions, which would be fair to the firemen, to those who use the railway, to the railway company, and to its other employees, should be observed by the railway for the purpose of protecting firemen now in its employ against the consequences of the loss of such employment and seniority therein?
(c)	Should the provisions in the present agreements between the railway company and the brotherhood concerning "arbitraries" and the "mountain differential" be maintained, dropped or modified, and if in the opinion of the commission they should be modified, how and to what extent?
2.	That the Hon. Mr. Justice Kellock be chairman of the commission:
3.	That the commissioners be authorized to exercise all the powers conferred upon them by section 11 of the Inquiries Act;-
That section authorizes them to engage counsel, experts or clerks, the staff they may require for the performance of their duties.
4.	That the commissioners be authorized to secure technical advice and assistance from the members and staff of the board of transport commissioners and from any other board, commission, agency or department of the government of Canada;
5.	That the commissioners be authorized to engage the services of such counsel, staff and technical advisers as they may require at rates of remuneration and reimbursement to be approved by the treasury board;
6.	That the commissioners adopt such procedure and methods as they may from time to time deem expedient for the proper conduct of the inquiry and sit at such times and places as they decide from time to time; and
7.	That the commissioners report to the governor in council.

It's all to the credit of the people of Canada, in the way of national culture.

Mr. Speaker, in common with other hon. members who have preceded me in this debate I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply upon their fine contributions to this debate. I am sure their

The Address-Mr. MacEachen constituents had every reason to appreciate the distinction with which the important task assigned to them was discharged.
I believe that we as representatives of the people of Canada are in position to express gratification over the continued economic expansion of this nation, an expansion which is likely to bring increasing material rewards and provide cultural and spiritual opportunities for an ever-growing number of Canadians. I noted that yesterday in his excellent address the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre pointed out that one of the chief domestic problems in this country was the problem of inflation. It is interesting to remember that for a 20-year period prior to 1940 the chief preoccupation of all democratic assemblies in every part of the world was the problem of deflation or mass unemployment.
I think at the present time we have every justification for feeling that the concentrated research and efforts made to overcome the problem of mass unemployment have yielded great results, and that in Canada in the future we are not likely to face this type of terrible dislocation. If that is so, I venture to suggest that in the future this parliament will show a growing concern that the fruits of our economic abundance shall be more fully shared by all classes and regions of this country.
Gross national product, net national product, national income, disposal income; all these are growing beyond the wildest expectations, and as aggregate measures of our national welfare are quoted to show that Canadians are better off than ever before. However, we are not representatives of economic aggregates, we are representatives of people. Although we rejoice at the general growth in our economy, we would be derelict in our duty and responsibility if we did not take measures to guarantee that all classes and regions of the country share in the general prosperity.
I wish at this point to express my appreciation to the government and especially to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour for bringing an end to the railway strike. The settlement was reached through the process of mediation and within the procedures of free collective bargaining. I am glad the government refrained from imposing a settlement in this situation. However, although the settlement of the strike makes us all breathe easier, there are still issues remaining resulting from this important national incident.
It seems to me that the railway strike has focused attention on a very important aspect of collective bargaining, namely the relationship between free collective bargaining

and the public interest or national welfare. We in this country believe in the process of free collective bargaining. We believe that employers and employees should settle their disputes by negotiation, mediation or ultimately through inflicting economic losses on the other party through a strike or lockout. These procedures are at the very root of our conception of free collective bargaining. Indeed in the United States those assumptions were explicitly written in the first Wagner act.
It would be a bad thing for free labour and free enterprise in this country if the procedures of collective bargaining were impaired or destroyed. At the same time, what made this strike so important in the field of collective bargaining was the feeling that in some way the national welfare or the public health and safety of the nation were threatened. As I said at the outset, the conflict presented by this strike was in a sense a conflict between the continued exercise of free collective bargaining and the interests of the nation as those interests are reflected in the health and welfare of its citizens.
In this case because of the intervention of the Prime Minister the strike did not move to its final conclusion, nor was there any imposition of compulsory arbitration. Nevertheless the issue still remains, and it seems to me that when the passion and prejudice of a strike of this kind disappear the whole problem of the emergency or the public welfare aspect should become the subject of investigation by the industrial relations committee of this house.
Other states, particularly in the United States, have made some effort to deal with the emergency aspect. I refer in particular to legislation of the state of New Jersey. In that legislation definite procedures are laid down setting forth the method by which the state can cope with emergency disputes. One of the real problems in this whole area is to define what is actually an emergency dispute, in other words what type of dispute threatens the public interest and the health and welfare of the nation.
Under the New Jersey act a 60-day cooling and mediation period is provided for, including hearings, in connection with all labour disputes in "public utilities." Of course that phrase is subject to very broad definition. Seizure and compulsory arbitration may be invoked if any strike, work stoppage or lockout in the opinion of the governor might result in the failure to continue the operation of a public utility and threaten the public interest, health and welfare.
It is very difficult to define exactly what strike will actually threaten public interest,

health and welfare. Certainly every strike involves economic losses. In many strikes involving non-public utilities there are very grave and heavy economic losses. As an illustration of the difficulty of defining the nature of public emergency I should like to refer to a strike which occurred in New Jersey in 1947, when the employees of the Bell Telephone system went on strike and completely interrupted the telephone service. The attorney general of New Jersey stated:
It is of course axiomatic that the telephone service is essential in the life of present-day civilization.
Later the supreme court of New Jersey agreed that in the economic and social life of today a method of communication such as the telephone was a vital and indispensable essential to the health, safety and welfare of the public. On the other hand, in the state of Massachusetts the governor, who at that time had a very outstanding labour management committee, asked an opinion of this body and they held that the absence of the telephone service would not jeopardize the public health and public safety.
The first problem in this particular area is to determine just what type of strike is involved, the magnitude of the economic loss and whether the extent of the inconvenience caused to the public would be such as to impair the public health and safety. I have not heard or read of any serious effort in this particular dispute to set forth the elements of what truly constitutes a national emergency arising from a labour dispute.
There has been a great deal said in this house and elsewhere both for and against the imposition of compulsory arbitration, and in discussing compulsory arbitration it seems to me the first consideration is the effect that compulsory arbitration is likely to have on collective bargaining itself. The best studies made of the experience in New Jersey reflect the opinion that instead of making agreement through negotiation easier, compulsory arbitration makes negotiation more difficult for both parties and undermines to some extent the process of collective bargaining. This is because, first of all, the disputants prepare for arbitration rather than for negotiation. The second reason-and all agree on this; labour, management and state-is that any reasonable effort made to reach a settlement by one party is usually taken by the other as a basis for bringing the dispute to arbitration in order to get a better settlement.
In Canada we have a set of rules applicable to collective bargaining in general, but no special set of rules which apply to both
The Address-Mr. MacEachen public utilities and emergency disputes. The whole area is very clouded and subject to a great deal of confusion. My own opinion is that it is not a healthy situation in the field of collective bargaining to have uncertainty with regard to the method of settling such disputes, and to have the whole argument reaching the Prime Minister's office where only the prestige and the skill of the Prime Minister himself can be used to provide the final momentum in settling difficulties of this nature.
I can think of no better subject for study by the industrial relations committee of this house than this problem of emergency disputes and the best possible procedure that can be used to settle them, consistent with the preservation of the best interests of free collective bargaining.
Mr. Speaker, many members of this house have already referred to the royal commission on economic prospects, and its report has become the subject of discussion all over Canada. It has been of particular interest to the Atlantic region, because many people from the Atlantic provinces felt that this commission would do for Canada what the Rowell-Sirois commission did for this country at an earlier period. The Rowell-Sirois commission, I believe, presented an economic and moral defence for the present fiscal arrangements and the present welfare community which has strengthened and made possible the continuation of the federation in this country.
It was my own feeling that the Gordon commission would attempt to set forth a particular program of economic redevelopment in the Atlantic provinces combined with a series of policy recommendations that could become the basis of legislative action by this parliament. The royal commission does recognize the necessity of such an approach to the problems of the Atlantic region. It states as follows:
What is required is a positive and comprehensive approach to the problems of the Atlantic region. With this as an objective it is suggested that the people of Canada as a whole might be willing to assist the people of the Atlantic provinces in discovering, developing and making the best use of resources in that area.
It is very hard to make fair comment on the suggestions in this section of the report in the absence of the supporting studies of the commission and, in particular, in the absence of the analyses which guided the commissioners in reaching their conclusions.
I am particularly interested in awaiting the study and contribution by Dr. Howland on the regional aspects of Canada's economic development. However, I believe general disappointment was felt that the Gordon

The Address-Mr. MacEachen commission had failed to present at this stage a general program for maritime economic development.
The expectations of many, including myself, were not realized in this report. There is no integrated program for maritime redevelopment; there is no examination of the commercial and monetary policies pursued by the government that might have a favourable or adverse effect on the economy of the Atlantic region. And finally, there are no recommendations for stimulating the private sector of the economy in the Atlantic region.
I have a feeling that the commission, for some reason, is out of step with the objectives of the Atlantic provinces economic council, which is now beginning a very comprehensive effort to solve some of the problems of the maritime region.
I hope the commissioners, who yet have to complete their final report, will remedy what seems to me to be a very vital deficiency in the preliminary report, namely the absence of a comprehensive and integrated program which might form the basis of maritime recovery.
Nevertheless there are one or two things mentioned in the commission's report which might form the basis for some discussion. The commission recommends the setting up of a capital projects commission to which the federal government would be expected to make annual contributions, and from which might be expected to evolve recommendations as to how public projects should be developed in the Atlantic region.
I cannot comment for the province of Newfoundland or, indeed, for any other province, but it seems to me that in the field of public projects the Atlantic region, or at least the province of Nova Scotia, has made the greatest headway. The federal government has already provided substantial capital assistance to public projects which merited consideration, among them the Canso causeway, the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry and other schemes that come to mind. The suggestion of the commission would, it seems to me, simply make more formal the arrangement which already exists, and is likely to lead to difficulties in reconciling the various needs and requirements of the four governments who would form the group in the capital projects commission.
The commission itself lays great stress on the problem of transportation, and calls for a trunk highway system in the Atlantic region. Here again, in the field of road building and the provision of important links in our transportation system, to which I have already referred, considerable progress has been made in the Atlantic region.
	!
One problem mentioned by the Gordon commission was the inadequacy of the present transportation arrangements between North Sydney and Port aux Basques and the alleged bottleneck that exists in the transport of freight between Port aux Basques and North Sydney. I have had occasion already to suggest to the Department of Transport that an alternative steamship service be established between the Avalon peninsula and Port Hawkesbury on Cape Breton island. As you know, the construction of the Canso causeway has resulted in the creation of an all-year port at Port Hawkesbury, and its outstanding possibilities could be used in the setting up of this alternative steamship service. I realize that the commission suggested that the alternative service might be set up between Halifax and St. John's, but I am sure the members from Halifax will generously allow this steamship service to be rerouted to my constituency.
The commission placed great emphasis on the lower income levels that exist in the Atlantic area, and it is true that the level of income is lower in that area than in the rest of Canada. The commission goes on to suggest that several methods could be adopted to overcome this disparity in income levels, and one of the final suggestions made reads as follows:	,
Any serious attempt to raise income levels in the Atlantic provinces will soon break down into consideration of a series of problems which must be dealt with separately and individually.
Then it suggests that among the problems are matters which come within the general administrative competence of the federal government or its agencies, on which favourable decisions could provide some modest measure of assistance to one or other of the Atlantic provinces. I have a modest measure to propose to the government which I think will go some distance toward overcoming the disparity in incomes that now exists as between certain workers in the Atlantic region and in other parts of Canada. I refer to the prevailing rate employees of the federal government, particularly on the island of Cape Breton. I understand that under the procedure now in existence the Department of Labour strikes the prevailing rate that should be paid to federal employees, based on surveys, and then its recommendation is made to the various government departments.
I have in mind, for example, the employees at the Cape Breton highlands national park, Louisburg park, Point Edward naval base and, in the province of New Brunswick, the employees at Camp Gagetown. The employees in Cape Breton highlands national park receive an hourly compensation 30 to 35 per cent below the compensation paid to

equivalent workers in the province of British Columbia. This is so because the general wage level is lower in that area than in the province of British Columbia.
This policy of paying the prevailing rates accommodates itself to the lower wage rates existing in certain parts of Canada. I cannot see why we cannot pay a uniform rate to these employees as we do to civil servants and railway employees despite their location in the country. I believe the government should seriously consider paying a uniform rate to all prevailing rate employees in Canada. The uniform rate could be the equivalent of an average rate struck for the whole country, or the equivalent of the maximum rate existing in any particular labour market.
I know there are certain arguments in defence of the present policy. There are certain formidable arguments against it. For myself, I believe that our common Canadian citizenship should be a much more important factor in determining the rate of pay for government employees than our accidental presence in any particular labour market at any given moment. I urge the government to give serious consideration to the problem of prevailing rate employees, and to make an effort in this modest way to overcome some of the disparities that exist in income levels as between the Atlantic region and other parts of Canada.
I want to refer for a moment to the very welcome announcement made by the Prime Minister that a special study is to be undertaken of the problem of land use in this country. I have no doubt that such a study will inevitably lead to a consideration of the general economic forces determining the level of income for the farmers and the agricultural class of Canada. I am sure this opportunity so provided will result in a much wider understanding of some of the economic problems that are involved in getting higher incomes for the farmers of Canada. I must say that my own experience has been that on no other subject is there so much misunderstanding and confusion as there is on the economics of agriculture, and particularly the almost irreconcilable views that exist between the economists of agriculture and the philosophers of agriculture. I hope this opportunity will permit a meeting of minds between the economists and the philosophers, so that some agreed policy can be followed with wide public support that will provide to those who wish to farm a return commensurate to that of people in other occupations in Canada.
I had the opportunity just before leaving for Ottawa to have a discussion with the
The Address-Mr. MacEachen executive of the Inverness county farmers' association, and these men asked me to put forward two matters in the House of Commons. I believe the government intends to continue its present policy with respect to assistance on the movement of feed grains to eastern Canada. This policy has been of considerable advantage to the farmers of Nova Scotia, and they wish to have it continued as a permanent policy of the government.
The second problem brought to my attention is a problem that has been mentioned in the house before, and which has to do with the conservation of agricultural lands, particularly along the rivers of my constituency. There are many acres of valuable meadow land now being carried away because there is no provision by which the federal government, the provincial governments and the owners themselves can co-operate in a policy of conservation. I believe this is an immediate problem, and that it does not require the extended deliberations of a Senate committee to have some arrangements by which we shall conserve some of the best meadow land, certainly in my part of Canada and I am sure the same applies to other parts as well.
I have been interested in the discussions which have taken place on the subject of social security, and in particular the suggestions made in the house that the old age security payment be increased. I wish to assure my colleagues in the house that I have not been tipped off by the government or by anybody else as to the probable course of action that is to be followed in this matter. I prefer to be tipped off by the feeling of my own constituents, and in this case I can honestly say that of all the areas of need there is none which gets a greater response among the citizens of my constituency than any proposal to assist in a greater measure the older citizens of this country.
I would remind the house that the persons who are now in receipt of old age security in Canada are persons who were subject, in the course of their working and earning lives, to some of the greatest depressions and dislocations in our economy, and in many cases they are those who worked without the protection of improved legislation and without the protection of trade unions; whose earning capacity, certainly in their working years was much less than the earning capacity of their fellow citizens today. Here is one place where I feel that the usual sympathy with which this government treats those citizens can be very usefully employed.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, and I want to say this in conclusion, that the chief reproach

The Address-Mr. Jones made against this government by the official opposition has been a reproach that it is lacking in leadership, that the Prime Minister and his ministers have failed to provide the necessary leadership in this country. Each member of the house, and each citizen of this country, will wish to decide for himself the confidence he places in this government. For myself I believe that the Prime Minister in his magnificent intervention in the Suez debate, and later in the debate on the address in reply, has shown himself to be a leader in the proper sense of leadership, that is leadership tempered by wisdom and long experience; and his understanding and vigour in the solution of the railway strike were, to me, considerable evidence of leadership.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs certainly needs no recommendations from any member of this house. His real leadership in the United Nations has earned the respect of all countries of the world, and he has shown himself to be a skilful and resourceful champion of peace in a manner that achieves practical results. Recently all of us were grieved and saddened at the very horrible events which occurred in Hungary, and in the press of this country there were admonitions and fears that the government would not respond properly to this challenge. I noticed recently that the editorial writers, from whom it is often difficult to extract any praise, have given the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration considerable praise and approval for the manner in which he has responded to this problem. Finally the Minister of National Health and Welfare has returned from a mission which again shows the manner in which the government is working to protect the interests of this country at home and abroad.
In the light of these few instances which I have cited, and there are others which could be mentioned, this government is certainly deserving of the confidence of the house; and I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that I will not hit the headlines by announcing that I intend to support the government in all the votes precipitated by this debate.

Mr. Speaker, like other speakers who have preceded me I must express my disappointment with the omissions from the throne speech of such important subjects as old age pensions, blind pensions, national health grants and so forth. But in spite of that I was rather pleased that it included one item which I was very anxious to see brought into effect; that is the extension of the Municipal Grants Act. I would like to compliment the minister for introducing it at this time. To my mind it' meets a moral and legal
[Mr. MacEachen.l

responsibility of the government which they have evaded for many years. In spite of that, I would like to offer one or two criticisms of the act. I hate to look a gift horse in the mouth but to my mind grants, while welcome, are not the solution to municipal-federal relations in this field.
Many years ago the union of British Columbia municipalities condemned grants in aid in general as a very unsatisfactory way to recompense a municipality for any service rendered, on the ground that those grants can and do vary from year to year, and they can be withheld or increased or decreased at the whim of the government. It almost reminds you of a mother trying to train her child by offering candy; a little more if he is better and a little less if he is not, and so on, forgetting that eventually he will become an adult.
That is the trouble with the federal government. The municipalities are just as capable of handling their own affairs and finances as the federal government is in its field. I feel, therefore, that the federal government is not the body which should determine the value of the service given by the municipalities. I do not suppose this grant will have any relationship to that service, because the federal government is not in a position to assess it. Therefore I suggest that the municipality should make the assessment. For that reason the federal government should take full responsibility for all municipal taxes on all federal properties within the municipalities, just as any other taxpayer or any businessman has to do. In this way the municipalities could budget properly which cannot be done with the uncertain type of grants in aid. The government then would be assuming a responsibility which to my mind they have been evading for many, many years.
I was going to talk a little about agriculture this afternoon. When I mention agriculture most of you will immediately think of wheat, but I -wish to remind hon. members that there are other important branches of agriculture, such as cattle and dairying, and so on. There is also what the government seems to regard as the Cinderella of the farm groups, and I refer to the fruit and vegetable growing industries. The Cinderella group is waiting at the present moment to try on a glass slipper. It may prove that it will be the right size. I refer to the provincial royal commission which is starting to work in British Columbia at the present time. They are going to investigate the problems affecting the fruit and vegetable industry of that province, but not of the whole of Canada. I hope when the investigation is finished and

the recommendations are made the story will have the same happy ending as the original Cinderella fairy tale.
I regret that the federal government could not see its way clear to join with our province in establishing a federal-provincial royal commission so the benefits of that commission could have been extended to other fruit and vegetable growing areas of Canada. In spite of the failure of the government to enter into a royal commission pact, the Minister of Agriculture has promised that he will give full support in supplying data and other information for the use of this commission. When those data have been submitted and the findings of the commission have been made we want sympathetic assistance from the federal government at the time it will be needed, because I am satisfied that the findings will include matters affecting the federal government, such as freight rates, tariffs, dumping, export policies, and so on.
I have not the time today to go into details, but I can assure the minister that these subjects will be and must be adjusted satisfactorily before we can restore a healthy economic condition to our fruit and vegetable industry. I would point out that the growers are not asking for charity; they are merely asking for a chance to acquire their fair share of the national income, which they certainly are not getting at the present time. As I pointed out to the house once or twice, their economic burden has been greatly increased by the loss of very valuable fruit trees which were killed by frost last year and one or two years before that. It will take many years to re-establish the trees on those farms so they will again be profitable to the growers.
Personally I feel that both the federal and provincial governments should have offered assistance to the fruit growers to help them through their period of difficulty, but so far neither government has done so, with the exception of the help given by the federal government to veterans whose farms had been ruined by frost. The federal government has started to try to help the veterans. How far it will go I do not know, but it has started.
As the royal commission is now starting to work on the problems of the fruit farmers, I will not take up the time of the house to discuss the matter in any detail at this time; but I should like to suggest to the minister that in future representatives of the fruit and vegetable growers of Canada as a whole be invited to appear before the agriculture committee of the house so the minister can hear from the operators and from the managers of the various organizations what the farm problems really are.
That is now done each year by the wheat growers. I support the wheat growers in
The Address-Mr. Jones their request to place before the government what they expect from the government. On the other hand, the fruit and vegetable growers are never invited to appear before the committee. As far as the committee is concerned it does not know that the fruit and vegetable growers exist. I would urge the minister to give them a chance to do this in the future. If it is done they can have their problems discussed. If it had been done in the past I am satisfied that the acute conditions in which they find themselves today could have been alleviated.
May I make one more suggestion to the minister. I am always pleased to praise the experimental farms in our province. They do good work on culture, on pruning, on farm practices and the use of by-products, but I should like to see the work extended. I should like to see another department to deal with marketing, transportation, packing and other matters vitally affecting the industry, placed under the experimental farms. The government could help immeasurably by adding a division to look after marketing, transportation and other problems of the fruit grower. The information obtained through an impartial and scientific study of marketing problems could be passed on to the fruit growers and it would be invaluable to them. Finally I would ask the minister to carry out his promise to give federal support to the investigation now taking place into the fruit industry of British Columbia.
I should like to deal briefly with the veterans. Their problem has been somewhat alleviated by the presentations made in this house by various veteran members, from time to time, but they have not all been ironed out. That is why I should like to draw the attention of the house to a copy of the Legionary which most hon. members must have received last week. I would ask the minister to study the excellent brief that the Canadian Legion recently presented to the cabinet. I do not intend to repeat the presentation here, but I do wish to endorse it. This brief was prepared by men who know the cost of war, who know that the present dangers may lead to war, who offered their lives for their country, and many of whom bear the scars of battle to this day. A brief prepared by such men deserves the closest study and attention by the government. I trust the cabinet realizes that and will act accordingly.
These men have made a close study of pensions as a whole, and have produced interesting comparisons of the increases in industrial compensation for services rendered since 1920 and the increases in war veterans pensions in the same period. I hope the minister will study the table. It

The Address-Mr. Jones is most interesting. One recommendation, if accepted, would solve a very difficult problem. I refer to the veteran who has difficulty in establishing his claim after neglecting for many years to make the claim. Oftentimes he is turned down on the ground that the injury or disease was of pre-enlistment origin. The Legion claim, and to my mind quite rightly, that the government through its officials, doctors and others, puts each recruit through a very comprehensive and rigorous examination, and when the recruit is finally accepted it is presumed, or should be presumed, that he is physically fit and in a healthy condition. I agree with the Legion when they claim that the government should, for pension purposes, abide by the findings of their own medical examiners at the time of enlistment.
I should like to read the recommendation covering this:
The Canadian Legion therefore recommends:
That section 13 (1) (a) of the Pension Act be amended so that, where a pension applicant who served in an actual theatre of war is found to have a disability resulting from an injury or a disease not recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment, such injury or disease shall be presumed to have occurred or had its inception subsequent to enlistment.
I think that is a very fair request. Most of their requests are on similar lines. I would mention one or two. One is:
That the ceilings on total permissible incomes under the War Veterans' Allowance Act be increased to $1,200 per year for the single recipient and $2,000 per year for the married recipient.
Another is:
That the married rate of war veterans allowance be increased from $108 per month to $120 per month.
A further one is:
That Canadian veterans of world war I whose overseas service was restricted to the United Kingdom be eligible for war veterans allowance, provided that such service be at least one year in duration.
I will read just one more:
That widows of allied ex-servicemen be granted war veterans allowance in cases where the husband died before completing 20 years' residence in Canada, provided:
(a)	that the effective date of her eligibility be 20 years after the husband's arrival to take up permanent residence in Canada;
(b)	that the widow herself has completed 20 years' residence in Canada, and
(c)	that the husband and wife were both otherwise eligible.
I would pass on these recommendations of the Legion to the minister and the cabinet. I think they are modest and deserving and the Legion is not asking for anything more than the country as a whole is willing to give them. There are other recommendations, but I do not have time to go into them more fully. I sincerely hope the minister will do

his utmost to put that brief into effect in order to carry out the wishes not only of the returned men alone but of every Canadian who feels obliged to the returned men for the service rendered on his behalf in protecting his home.
Before concluding I should like to mention old age and blind pensions. Like other hon. members of this house I have recently received numerous letters pleading with me as a member to do something on their behalf and outlining the difficulty they have in making ends meet. I am not going into the details of these problems, because you know them as well as I do; but they are serious problems, particularly those of the blind pensioners who have a severe handicap to begin with, plus the handicap imposed upon them by the small amount of their pension cheques.
The suggestion that the increase be made this year has already received support from all sides of the house, the Liberals, the official opposition, the Social Crediters and members of the C.C.F. party, and in addition it has the wholehearted support of all Canadians; for the need of a decent and satisfactory old age and blind pension is well known to every one of us. The least we can do is to keep on urging the government to assume this responsibility and alleviate the misery of these blind and old people by giving them a reasonable standard of living. Some of them cannot possibly get by on the present pension, and live on the charity of friends and relations. In many cases their lives are shortened because they do not have the wherewithal to buy sufficient sustenance. They are another group who, like the veterans, are deserving of a fairer share of our national economy. The aged are the pioneers who laid the groundwork which enabled our economy to reach its present standard; therefore to my mind they have a rightful claim to a far larger portion of the national economy which they helped to create.
I do not feel I am asking for too much when I request that immediate consideration be given to these matters. Do not use this as bait to gain votes at the election, because that will lose for you many friends. I am now referring to the minister or the cabinet, whichever you like, but I would urge in the name of common humanity and common justice that you immediately increase both the old age and blind pensions.

It gives me a great deal of pleasure to follow a fellow countryman in this debate, a young man who was born in the north of Ireland and travelled across the Atlantic and across this country as far as Edmonton from where he was sent back here to serve her most gracious

The Address-Mr. Mclvor
majesty; who has told her that we dearly love her and are going to do what we can to maintain Canada as a leading nation. I congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) on his splendid speech. I also would like to congratulate the other Irishman who seconded the motion. I should like to refer again to the hon. member for Regina City; he is a big fellow, and I know he will not mind. When the strike was on he said the government was doing nothing, that they were sitting back waiting for something to turn up. If this strike has settled anything, it has settled two things.

The Address-Mr. Mclvor First, the government, especially three members in the persons of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Trade and Commerce went all out in their efforts to settle the strike. The second thing this strike has shown is that the Canadian Pacific and the union officials are reasonable men who believe in co-operation.
I should like to offer a little advice, which I hope will be passed on to them. The C.P.R. officials, the C.N.R. officials and the officials of the Canadian Labour Congress would do well to get together and co-operate so there will never be another strike. They should realize the loss of business there has been because of the competition from highway and water transport. They must co-operate; they must work together.
I submit that strikes can be eliminated in three ways; first, by honest co-operation; second, by giving the men a share in the profits. This has worked out quite well in two places in Fort William, and if it works in Fort William it will work in Regina. The third way by which strikes could be eliminated would be by the application of the golden rule. This is the sure way. When you have that you have happy people working together.
I should like to say a word about northwestern Ontario. I remember when I first came down here I was told that all we had at the head of the lakes were big trees, big rocks, summer resorts and 40 below temperatures, all things that did not mean very much to the rest of Canada. That has all been changed. I would refer hon. members to Trade and Commerce magazine, and an article which appears on page 17 dealing with northwestern Ontario. This article indicates that nearly $400 million is to be spent in the expansion of primary industries of forest and mine and the development of electric power. It indicates that there is unprecedented growth all over northwestern Ontario. The government of the province of Ontario, under the leadership of Premier Frost, have certainly taken off their coats and gone to work in northwestern Ontario. Even though they are Conservatives they are doing a good job.
Fort William is leading in the development of northwestern Ontario. At the beginning of the year the Abitibi people announced they were going to expend $20 million in additions to their pulp and paper mill, and it is expected the expenditure will go beyond that. A gentleman came up from Quebec to manage the Great Lakes company, and it is noted that under his leadership they will erect the largest paper mill in the world. The first announcement was that there would be an expenditure of $40 million, but

it is now indicated that the expenditure will be $80 million. They will have the largest wood yard in the world at Fort William.
Activities at Canada Car are becoming more steady all the time. They have had one million accident-free hours, which indicates co-operation between the workers and the management. They have received a contract for 250 diesel buses for the Montreal tramways commission. Just think what that will mean to a city which is growing by leaps and bounds.
Our city council supported the Hungarian committee and has agreed to receive refugees. We are very proud of that. Donald Clark and Sons, who purchased the Great Lakes sawmill, which has been idle for some time, have indicated that they will make available several houses in which workers used to be housed. We hear a great deal about the government going to the bow-wows. I hardly think that is so, because so many people outside of this country want to come to Canada. I will refer only to one group because of their characteristics. Four thousand Scotsmen every month want to come to Canada. Scotsmen are supposed to be sane and steady, with an eye for the future. Yet in the face of that fact an hon. member over there is likely to get up and say that we are going to the bow-wows.

It will not be out of power in my time, and I expect to live to be 100. I should like to tell the Minister of Finance how he can spend some cash. We have an old rink in Fort William which was purchased by the government and made into an armoury. It was a wooden building which had not been painted for 20 years, so you can imagine its condition. When I was showing the sights to visitors to Fort William I never took them there. We need a federal building, because the unemployment office is hard pressed for space. These people are located in the old post office. Under my late friend, Hon. Dr. Manion, a new post office was built and I had the job of putting somebody in the old building. I could not get anybody but a beer parlor to go in; then finally we handed it over to the Salvation Army for a rental of $1 per year. They were there for seven years.
The building was then taken back from the Salvation Army. I did not like it, but I do not say many bad words about the government because I want them to measure up.

They certainly did measure up. They gave enough for a down -payment on a new building, $2,600 which will provide a place for the army. Therefore the Minister of Finance can spend some money along that line.
There are two other things about which the government can do something and which I have been advocating for the past four years. One is pensions for veterans. I have quoted several cases of men who were in the front trenches for four Christmas dinners. When they came back they were discontented and not at all like themselves, and they found it hard to settle down. I say that men who were in the trenches that long should receive a pension at 60 years without a means test. These men gave their best; they risked everything. A lot of them did not come back. These men deserve an old age pension without a means test at 60 years.
Another thing I have been advocating and which I have referred to previously is the case of the civil servant who has been on a small salary and has been retired. I have a resolution on the order paper which reads:
That in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to increase the pensions of civil servants who were retired when salaries were low, so as to bring such pensions more in line with the present.
I have visited some of these homes, and it is a pitiable thing to see. They are clean and tidy and in fine shape, but the people living in them certainly do not get three meals a day as I do. I will not say any more on this subject because it will be dealt with again in a full dress debate. I have spoken to the hon. Minister of Finance, and he has assured me of that.
I remember that before the last election I had a resolution on the order paper for three years in succession asking for pensions for the handicapped. This request was well supported by everybody, especially by some hon. members who have since gone to the Senate. The government did not wait until this session to grant those pensions; they did it immediately after the election, and I am expecting that right after this election the civil servants will receive their increased pensions and also that the veterans will get their old age pensions at 60. I would like to speak for the blind, but that matter will come up again on the budget.
Before closing I would like to congratulate the government on the steady way in which they are doing things and on the reputation they enjoy in the country. We will be happy to welcome anybody either on this side of the house or on the other side, after the next election, to tell us just how all these things should be done.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate all the complimentary things the hon. member has said regarding the Irish. My forefathers came to this country from Ireland around 150 years ago and I consider myself a Canadian equal, almost, to any Canadian except for the redskins who were here before us.
I believe we members come to the House of Commons for the purpose of speaking our minds on the various subjects in which we should be interested, touching the welfare of our constituents and the well-being of Canada. Within the last few months the nations of the world have been confronted with some of the most momentous problems they have ever had to face. Nobody will deny that we have been close to global war, war which, had it occurred, would have brought unpredictable consequences.
We here in Canada belong to a very grand body of well-wishing people called the United Nations. We also belong to another community called the commonwealth of nations, the British commonwealth. If we had always had the type of man who was not too prone to forget what that word "British" means, we would have had today a commonwealth of united nations at which no country in the world would dare to shake a mailed fist. We were on the verge of having a commonwealth of nations which had within its orbit every raw material necessary to support the greatest combined group of countries in this world, a commonwealth containing Australia, New Zealand, the Malay States, South Africa, Canada and the British Isles.
These territories are rich in tin, wheat, cattle, metals and minerals of every type the world requires. All were to be found within the British commonwealth. We had the desire to help the wide world before we had set our own house in order. If we had done what we should all have been striving to do; if this had been accomplished; if we had worked more with the other members of the British commonwealth of nations; if we had speeded up our efforts, we could have gone to New York as members of the United Nations with a solid bloc of our people, speaking various languages but with a common purpose. We could have put our shoulders to the wheel and the combined effort would have made a tremendous difference to the whole United Nations set-up.
The two great nations of the world which have settled in Canada, and of whose people Canada is so proud, are France and the British Isles, England, Ireland and Scotland.

The Address-Mr. Ferguson Alongside these are, fortunately, a good sprinkling of the right type of people who came to these shores from other countries such as Germany, Italy and Holland. We are proud of the type of men who are called Canadians today, workers, men of vision, men who want this Canada of ours to have a population sufficient to become a real power in world affairs.
But a problem comes up in the United Nations, and what do we find? We find, to my chagrin and shame, that the representatives of Canada appointed by this government are going in with the group who are not closely knit with us. Some members of this group are, indeed, very far from us. The Russians are far away. The United States is not knit to us; it is near. They soon tell us they stand, alone, when the time comes for them to do so. Our representatives at the United Nations did not take the position: we are sorry; we know you must have had some good reason for this tremendous move in sending British and French troops to Egypt.
Oh, no. They did not take the sympathetic stand which one member of a family usually does with regard to another, even if the latter had stubbed his toe, as happens on some occasions. This attitude could have been taken and should have been taken. Our representative at the United Nations was glad to stand in with the Russians and the United States in condemnation of the two mother countries of this Canada of ours.
I am speaking my own mind and voicing my own opinions when I make this assertion, but many, many Canadians right across this country are ashamed from the tops of their hats to their shoes, over the action which was taken on behalf of Canada by Canada s representatives. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is a very great man; he is a highly educated man; he has handled himself and the affairs of Canada is a most masterly manner. But he should have kept his tongue in his cheek at the United Nations meetings when his own flesh and blood were up against the situation that confronted the great statesmen of the British Isles. They believed it was necessary to go into Egypt to save their very lives and the lives of the people of France. It was not simply an individual who took that step. It was thought out more carefully than the Secretary of State for External Affairs thought out some of the statements he made at the United Nations. People do not send thousands of men to probable death unless it is the last straw.
For my part, I would have loved to see the French and British troops go right into

Cairo and kick this dictator, Nasser, right into Russia where he belongs. That is my opinion. You are going to have to do something like that before this situation is cleared up. We now have the President of the United States telling us that he is going to do it when it suits him. I will tell you when he will do it. He will do it the minute that the oil needed by the United States is cut off, and he will not notify anybody.
If we are going on as we are our soldiers will be going to a war started by the United States and will be marching down Sparks street to the tune of Yankee Doodle. Yes, sir, the Yanks are coming. We will be cheered when we clear these people out of Egypt who are upsetting the entire equilibrium of this world, supported as they are by Russian munitions. When we liberate the people of Egypt the Yanks will be cheered and we will be included if we just keep going on as we are. That is not a very happy thought.
When France and England decided what they were going to do and did it Australia and New Zealand said: We are with you. I do not believe there is a man or woman in the House of Commons today who fears that if the British and French had gone on into Egypt the Russians would have dared to send any more munitions or any human beings anywhere in the Near East.
I saw some cartoons recently that were published in a leading Cairo paper prior to the people of Israel going into Egypt. One cartoon depicted a high, military shoe with a spur on it kicking a man with a pronounced Jewish expression on his face under the chin, kicking him out of the Near East. Another one from a leading Cairo daily paper showed a long knife dripping with blood and a chicken representing the people of Palestine with an incision in its throat and an agonized look. I am sure these cartoons were widely acclaimed by many people in Egypt who thought this great puppet and upstart, this imbecile ass, Nasser, would lead the Egyptians to conquer the world.
Nobody had the nerve to put their foot down two or three years ago when Nasser stopped the ships of Israel from going through the Suez canal, a waterway supposed to be open to all nations of the world. There is no doubt that the President of the United States knew of that situation. In my opinion, we have acquiesced in his requests for too long. British troops were taken away from the Suez canal. That was a nice, friendly gesture. They knew in their hearts that the right thing to do was to keep those troops there. But no, for the sake of a pacifist move

and because certain people would not face the realities of life these troops were removed from the canal area.
Lots of us will not face realities. Many times we do not do the right thing when we should and then we are confronted with an impossible situation. Let me tell you that the situation in the Near East prior to the British and French going into Egypt was an impossible one. It was not something you could fool with. What happened? At terrific expense the British and French moved in and then through the efforts of the representatives of the Canadian people at the United Nations and the efforts of the United States, not the little nations, the British and French were convinced that they should pull out for the sake of the peace of the world.
We are told that there are members of the British commonwealth who say they are going to withdraw from the commonwealth unless we let the Russians and the Egyptians run the better two-thirds of the empire. Well, if that is the kind of people they are the sooner they get out of the British commonwealth the better. Oh yes, my words are not ultra-diplomatic but they are the truth.

The time to voice our opinion on behalf of these people was at the right place, at the right time and for justifiable reasons. We had the justifiable reasons. When we go to the United Nations do we always have to be so diplomatic that we cannot express our views and what our hearts dictate? Must we turn on the friend who will forget our action, not resent it and still be our friend? It is the kind of deed where you kick a friend because you know he is a friend and is not going to put up much of a row about it and will say: Oh well, he did not mean it.
