The Address-Mr. Ferguson
Sir Anthony Eden and men of his calibre are saying, Oh, well, they did not mean it. Let me say to you that they did not need to do it. Our action has been misconstrued all over the face of the world to the detriment of the British commonwealth of nations and to the detriment of the free world.
It has been an incentive for a man like Nasser who tries to borrow money with one hand and who hits the donor with the other. It is the case of the dog that bites the hand that is feeding him. We are listening to that man. Here in Canada we are very proud of our regiment called the Queen's Own Rifles. We have every right to be proud of that regiment; they are the men who have defended the freedom of this country. The Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested with a great deal of pride that Canada would send troops to help keep the peace. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) who knew the great record of that famous regiment said, no doubt with pride, we are going to send a famous Canadian regiment, the Queen's Own Rifles. What happened? Let us face the facts. The Queen's Own Rifles were never sent because a puppet, a communist, a mean despicably-thinking man, a man who wants to cut the chicken's neck, said no.
I will say this about that Israel's chicken's neck; it is as good a neck as our neck, the neck to which Sir Winston Churchill referred. It was some neck when the hordes from Israel tore into Egypt. It was some neck and some chicken and the people of Egypt realize that today. They have $500,000 less in material that was shipped to them from Russia. Unfortunately at the present time the people of Israel are feeding 10,000 prisoners. If there is much more nonsense from that dictator I would certainly advocate that the people of Israel take another sock at them and clean them up properly. Do not let us just go home; in a few days let us not forget where the people of this country came from and where they started or how hard the battle was for our people to get in the position where we the people living in Canada today can say we have the most prosperous and progressive country in the world. It did not just grow on a tree, and we in the House of Commons had very little to do with putting us in the prosperous condition in which we are today and from which we are able to progress. We have been rather small contributors over the last 150 years. You have got to see just how much the last 20 years has contributed to the development of Canada. Let us go back a little further and give those people who hewed their homes out of the forests of this

The Address-Mr. Ferguson country the credit which they deserve. Let us try to unite the British commonwealth of nations. Let us try to stick together. Let us foster gatherings of representatives of all those nations. In the various parts of the empire let them know that we are with them. Let them know that we seek for them to be with us, and let them know that we stand together. There is no nation in the world would dare to try to put anything over an us. We would sleep a lot more soundly at night than we may sleep if the British commonwealth of nations is broken or if we neglect our old friends who fought with us in the last war and the first war. We had the Japanese and we had the Italians in the first war. In the last war they were our enemies.
That great nation of France was invaded by the destroying German hordes. They are the people who stood with us and lost hundreds of thousands of men in the first war. In the one battle they lost 250,000 of the flower of the nation, one battle, 24 hours. It takes centuries to recover that kind of blood and that kind of manpower. Do not let us forget that. We had every right to say to our old friend France-and I say our old friend because I know France has been our tried and true friend and the tried and true friend of the British Isles. If Canada had cabled and said we are with you and with your country, and has asked for volunteers for an army to help to defend the decision of the British government, you would get thousands of real Canadians as volunteers. But there would be a lot of them who would be reluctant to march behind the tune of a Yankee bugle.
While I am on my feet I just want to say a word about prosperity and about that terrific calamity which occurred in the United Nations due to the attitude of the government's representative. In various parts of Canada, particularly up in my own part of the country, we have people seeking to get roofs over their heads and to get out of the boarding houses and, in the case of young people, to get away from the old folks' home and to build homes of their own. Now, we talk about prosperity. All right. We have now reached, under the management of this government over the past 20 years, a prosperity in which you cannot pay for a home in 10 years. It takes 30 years, if ever. We have now reached a position where you cannot borrow the money necessary for a newly married couple to build a home and get a roof over their heads. The government tells us you can buy a house, or they have been telling us that for a long time. They say all


you have to do is go to the bank. After a lot of bickering and talking the banks have finally admitted that they will not make any more money available to young people to build houses.
Now, the manager of a bank operating in the town of Collingwood, where I come from, tells me, and I have asked the question several times, that they are not lending any more money for this purpose. That is prosperity. We are trying to curb that kind of prosperity. Let us curb something but do not curb the ability of people to get a roof over their heads. Let us scratch our heads so that we can get a thought as to how to overcome that obstacle, the obstacle of providing homes for the people of Canada. On the one hand we say, bring in immigrants, and I am heartily in accord with that. However, I hope they bring in men who are able to build houses and men who can lend money to the man who can only pay a reasonable amount down on a new home, so that he can proceed to build a new house. This condition exists across the country. People are not able to buy houses.
In the prosperity of today people are mortgaged to the hilt. The merchants in the smaller communities are finding business is not so good and when you inquire into it you find that the people are working but they are so heavily mortgaged that they will need to increase their wages before they are able to pay for the things which they are entitled to here in Canada such as refrigerators, electric stoves and automobiles. The average man who is willing to work should be able to have some of these commodities; they are not just luxuries, they are necessities. The automobile which you could buy in this country 12 years ago for $1,100 is now costing $2,600. The good home that you could buy for $5,000 is now costing $25,000. The bird cages which you are now getting are costing $15,000. When the young family move into a home now they get a warning, ' do not have any children because you will have to keep them out in the garage; there is no accommodation for them in the place. There is a living room, a bedroom and a kitchen. You could not swing a cat in it. It sells for $12,000 to $15,000. Well, that is prosperity. We must say something more than that we have prosperity. Unfortunately, people have learned to lean on the government to such an extent that the government finds itself in the position of having to be a guide and an aid to the great masses of Canada. We have the old age pension and unemployment insurance. Now there is talk of shorter working hours and more pay. Then, the commission the other day came out and

The Address-Mr. Ferguson
said, "Boys, a few years from now you are going to get $100 a week instead of $35 or $40. I had a carpenter working for me last week in Collingwood, doing some alteration on a building I own. He said, "Mr. J., we are going to have more employment in 25 years. Did you see where we are going to get $100 a week?" Well, I think I would have refrained from making that kind of statement if I had been on the commission. We all remember the difficult times we have gone through; all Canadians remember them. I do not know of any finer election statement that can be made prior to an election than that Canada is to have 25 years of uninterrupted prosperity. Unfortunately, the people of Canada are naive enough to believe statements of that kind.
The poor young fellow-he was a married man-who worked for me spoke of $100 a week and a 35-hour week. What a place to live in! I hope it comes true, but I would just as soon have $50 a week and be out of debt and pay for my home in 10 years rather than 30 years, and buy an automobile for $1,100 instead of paying $2,600 for almost the same kind of automobile. That is prosperity, all right, gentlemen; but we have to watch what we are doing. According to the press, the United States is paying two-thirds of its income on security. I do not know whether those figures include any money for the security of Canada; but if we keep on following them as we are doing we may have to look to them for money for our own security. We may have to ask, do you mind cutting us in on some of that because we have gone so far along the line that we cannot look after ourselves? We cannot even stand by our friends.
I should now like to deal with immigration. Since I have been in the House of Commons I have watched the various ministers of immigration. Shortly after the war this subject came up and the minister told us at that time that we needed immigrants. He said, "Canada is expanding, but we are short of ships". Well, we brought farmers out here, or men who said they were farmers. Many of them were school teachers, bookkeepers, nurses and so forth. They could not speak our language and had to learn it. After they had been here for one year they went back to their own vocations of life. I know a doctor and his wife from Rumania and Austria who served a sentence of one year washing dishes in Gravenhurst sanatorium. This graduate physician is now practising in Toronto. He will be able to tell his children when they grow up that his sentence was to come into this great country of ours, 82715-231
under the then existing immigration laws, and serve his term of one year washing dishes in the Gravenhurst sanatorium. That is the penalty that he had to pay. He will be able to say, "Son, are you not proud you are a Canadian, but I hope when you are old enough, and if you are able to reach parliament as a Canadian citizen, you will not penalize the people who want to come to this great country by making dishwashers out of doctors".
We have a trickle of immigrants coming to this country. There is a shortage of every kind of skilled labour in this country. I advertised in the Star and Telegram for two weeks for domestic help. I received three replies. All three admitted when I got in touch with them that they could not do the job but they just wanted to see what kind of job it might be. That is a reality. What is driving prices up? There is not enough good skilled labour to make labour properly competitive, and labour should be competitive. Efficiency increases in that way. Ever since the war this government has dilly dallied on the immigration question, which is one of the most vital questions in a growing country. We do not want farmers only; we want artisans of all kind, competent, honest, willing workers. We must plan the conditions under which they can be brought here under which they can be handled. We must have a strong and brainy, intelligent man in charge of the department to carry out the duties of that department in that manner. We do not want a man in charge of the department of immigration in this country who is criticized by the law society of the country; we do not want that type of man. He must be a competent and capable leader, and an exceedingly good businessman. He must be capable of co-operating with all other departments. The department of immigration is not the smallest of all the departments of a nation of 15 million people.
In the year 1957 in this great country of ours we have foreign capital developing this country so that our people continue to be hewers of wood and drawers of water. That is Liberal prosperity. I say that Canada is enjoying the greatest era of a certain type of prosperity that it has ever enjoyed. Millions of dollars are coming in from the United States, from Switzerland, from Germany, from England and from France. They are pouring in to develop our resources simply to give our people jobs, but in very few instances are they providing the cream of the profit to keep our people living over and above the old age pension. That is what we must have. We must have something

The Address-Mr. Carter more than the satisfaction of saying to a man, at the end of your efforts do not forget that you can get $40 a month to keep yourself in comfort here in Canada.
While I am on this subject may I say- I am speaking for myself-I think $40 a month is a disgrace. It is something we should not let happen. It could be changed quite easily. If an increase were proposed by this government it could be passed in 15 minutes, unanimously, I hope, to put the aged people, who served this country so well, in a position to have a slight degree of comfort in the final years of their lives so that they would not be seeking food in garbage cans when they are not depending on their families to look after them and feed them.
Every member of parliament knows how much the cost of living has increased. What effort has been made by the government to increase by a fraction the old age pension? Members of parliament know the price of automobiles as well as anybody in Canada knows it and we know the price of roast beef; not everyone does because they cannot afford it. We know that the price of food, clothing and housing is going up. Has this government stopped in its tracks and said, "This is going to be difficult. There is one group of people whom we cannot neglect any longer". I refer to the people who helped Canada become the great nation she is, the people who cannot now fend for themselves. I am speaking on behalf of every old mother who produced great Canadians for the future who is now hobbling along the street in ill health forced to live in a cold and bleak home in the city of Toronto, Montreal or elsewhere, eking out an existence on $40 a month, when we all know in our hearts that this sum is not adequate.
I am not asking for a luxury but for an increase that is long overdue. This is something that should be done without further procrastination, without further debate or political promises, long before the election- now.
Mr. Speaker, I have simply voiced my opinion here today on some subjects which are of great concern to me personally.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at the very beginning to associate myself with the very fine and well deserved tributes which have been paid to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne in recognition of the excellent manner in which they have discharged their duties. By the high order of their speeches and the manner


in which they were delivered they have enhanced the tradition of this chamber and reflected credit both on themselves and on their constituencies.
The speech from the throne refers to many matters which are of particular interest to my province and to my constituency. Apart from international affairs and economic developments which directly concern all Canadians from coast to coast there are three items dealing with education which show that the government recognizes both the vital necessity of attaining the maximum development of our human resources and the problems associated with it. The proposals to set up a Canada council for the arts, humanities and sciences, to double the grants for universities and to increase and improve grants for vocational and technical education will be heartily welcomed in my province and I believe by right thinking people in all parts of Canada. The extension of the scope of municipal grants, the plan to set up a Senate committee for the better use of land for agriculture and the proposed revision of the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act to provide a better scale of benefits to disabled seamen and the dependents of deceased seamen are three other measures of special interest to Newfoundland and to my own constituents. There will be opportunities for more extended remarks when these measures are brought before the house. At this time I wish merely to enumerate them and to commend the government for putting them on the agenda for this session.
Another item of special interest to all Canadians and particularly to the Atlantic provinces is the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects commonly known as the Gordon report. I do not think we should criticize this report too hastily; after all, it is merely a compilation of facts and deductions. Some of the conclusions reached may be disappointing to us and possibly disagreeable but I feel we must accept the report as an honest appraisal of present economic trends and the results that are likely to ensue if these trends are permitted to continue throughout the next quarter century. We are not required to agree with the opinions expressed nor with the assumptions on which they are based; after all, they could very well be mistaken. At best they can hardly be expected to be more accurate than a long-term weather forecast. We should not therefore accept the predicted results as inevitable; rather, we must see to it that the necessary action is taken in time to prevent those results, which we consider undesirable, from taking place.

In compiling a report of this kind and particularly when formulating recommendations or policy based on the findings, care must be exercised to make certain that purely material and economic considerations are not permitted to override human considerations and the over-all national interest. For example, the report confirms the fact that in the Atlantic provinces per capita and per family annual incomes are some 30 plus per cent lower than the national average. This tremendous discrepancy is rendered still worse by the fact that the cost of living in the Atlantic provinces is considerably higher than the national average. In my own province of Newfoundland this gap is at its widest.
What is the answer to this situation? On a purely material and economic basis the solution could be to encourage a movement of the population from the Atlantic provinces to the central provinces and it should be borne in mind that this sort of migration on a voluntary basis has always existed. But would any sane person maintain that it would be in the national interest to have the Atlantic provinces completely denuded? Where then should the line be drawn? What does the national interest demand? Surely the national interest demands that measures be taken to close the gaps in annual income and the cost of living so that material living standards in the Atlantic provinces will compare more favourably with the rest of Canada. This does not necessarily mean handouts but it does mean, first and foremost, that ways must be found and the necessary assistance must be provided to enable the people of the Atlantic provinces to raise their own living standards through their own efforts by developing their own resources to the maximum.
It would appear that present credit restrictions tend to retard the industrial development of the Atlantic provinces more than that of other parts of Canada thus producing the greatest effect where it is least needed. No one can deny the necessity of credit restrictions and other measures to offset the present danger of inflation, but what seems to be required is a more flexible way of applying them so that developments may be restricted in those areas where its contribution to inflation is greatest, and permitted or even encouraged in other areas where its effect will be slight. In this way the effects of anti-inflationary measures will be distributed more evenly throughout the nation. It should be borne in mind that the differential in individual annual income and living costs between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada is due to some extent to the fact that confederation changed their flow
The Address-Mr. Carter of trade from its normal and natural direction of north and south and compelled it to flow in the unnatural direction of east and west.
It can therefore be regarded as a price which the Atlantic provinces have been paying to make the concept of a Canadian nation a reality. The relative effects of this imposed disadvantage upon living standards and industrial and economic development have increased over the years and now represent a very real sacrifice on the part of the people of the Atlantic provinces. True it is a sacrifice which must be made in the national interest, but it is also one which benefits other parts of Canada and for that reason is entitled to recognition and compensation.
Whatever compensation resulted from the Maritime Freight Rates Act has been completely nullified by the recent freight increases, and simple justice demands that steps be taken to restore the maritime freight rates assistance to its original proportions.
We all know that our railways serve a purpose that is far more important than any economic consideration. Actually their east-west direction makes them economic monstrosities, but that east-west direction is essential to the national interest because it is our railways more than anything else that bind us together in a nation and make possible our political independence and economic autonomy as well as our economic growth and development.
The primary function of our railways is to integrate the different industrial sections of every province into a single provincial economy, and also to integrate the different provincial economies into a national economy. As far as Newfoundland is concerned, the Canadian National Railways are not performing either of these functions and will never be able to perform them as long as they maintain their present pattern.
We all want our railways systems to be operated as far as possible in accordance with sound business practices. I use this qualification because purely dollar considerations must not be permitted to take precedence over the over-all national interest and basic human needs. Since the railways are not basically sound enterprises within themselves as economic units, and since they have other functions even more important than the economic, I believe it would be better if they were regarded as public utilities. Certainly it would be better in Newfoundland.
The railways could be used as an effective instrument in equalizing the cost of living in

The Address-Mr. Carter different parts of Canada. In Newfoundland the Canadian National Railways create inequalities in living costs and make existing ones even worse. On Friday last my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten), placed on Hansard at page 136 figures to illustrate how the recent freight increase of 11 per cent has resulted in an actual freight increase of 64 per cent to the consignee at St. John's, Newfoundland. I am not going to repeat what he so clearly and concisely stated but I want to give my unqualified support to everything he said. I wish also to add my plea to his that the government of Canada adjust the rates of payment under the policy of freight assistance on western grains and mill feeds shipped to eastern Canada in order to bring these rates once more in line with the 1956 rate increases.
Before I leave this subject of railways I must once again, as I have done on several previous occasions, raise my voice in this chamber in protest against the lack of passenger accommodation provided by Canadian National Railways on their Placentia bay service. I have brought this condition to the attention of the Canadian National Railways management repeatedly over the past six years and it has been consistently ignored.
Every time I travel on the M/V Burin I am scandalized at the conditions which the travelling public are forced to put up with in this part of my riding. Picture women and children being forced to sit up all night in stormy weather huddled together on a bench in a tiny dining room or sitting on their luggage in a narrow corridor because there is no place for them to lie down. This prime example of man's inhumanity to man is a disgrace, not only to Canadian National Railways but to Canada. It makes me ashamed that the half million dollars required for a new ship should be regarded as being of more importance than human beings. It makes my blood boil to see a crown company treating human beings, and Newfoundlanders at that, with less consideration than one would normally give to dumb animals. Not only has this situation been permitted to continue, but it has steadily worsened for six long years, and I plead with the government to bring pressure to bear on the Canadian National Railways to have it corrected immediately.
I would ask the government also to give sympathetic consideration to the plight of those railway employees who have received notice of the termination of their employment. Some of these employees are over 50 years of age and are practically unemployable elsewhere. Furthermore, many of them stand to lose their pension rights which they have

accumulated over a long period of satisfactory service. Apart altogether from the terms of union, it is our Christian duty to see that their livelihood is not jeopardized because people are always more important than things. Therefore I urge the government to remove the suspense which has been hanging over the heads of these employees since 1949 by having their positions clearly defined so that they will know exactly where they stand.
Last Monday we were privileged to hear two excellent speeches-one by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) who has done so much to raise Canada's prestige among the nations of the world, and the other by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) who has just returned from a tour of Asia and Australasia where he has rendered outstanding service in building up mutual understanding and good friendly relations between Canada and the free nations of the east.
In both these great speeches the underlying theme was the importance of the human individual; that the individual worth of every human being for himself alone as a person should be recognized irrespective of colour, race or class; that human rights and human dignity should be preserved and maintained and along with human needs be given priority over every other consideration. This is the basic foundation of our western civilization. Our allegiance to those values marks the fundamental difference between western democracy and other forms of government. It is also the cornerstone of true liberal philosophy, and it is within this framework that we must examine the recommendations contained in the Gordon report and formulate future policy. There must be this fundamental consistency between our domestic policy on the one hand and our foreign policy on the other. While encouraging and assisting other nations in their efforts to correct the adverse effects of so-called colonialism we must take care we do not permit another brand of colonialism to develop within our own borders. The idea behind the Colombo plan is a noble conception which deserves our fullest support.
This concept would be still further enhanced and its effects as a moral force would be multiplied many times over by the concurrent existence of a Colombo type plan for the underdeveloped areas of our own nation. Such a program is necessary for the maximum development of the fishing industry not only of Newfoundland but of all the Atlantic provinces, which industry must in my opinion be developed in an orderly manner as a single

unit and not as a number of separate small industries fighting among themselves and competing with each other.
No thinking person would maintain that it is in the best interests of Canada or of the world to permit this vast treasure house of self-perpetuating wealth to remain underdeveloped or undeveloped, particularly at a time when four-fifths of the people of the world are underfed and undernourished. Maximum development of the fishing industry is a responsibility which we owe to the rest of the world, and it can come about only by the co-ordinated efforts of private industry, provincial governments and the federal government working together as a team with a passion and a plan.
We can be justly proud, Mr. Speaker, that many of the nations are today looking to Canada for moral leadership. In meeting that challenge let us never forget that peace can never be created by organizations or alliances, however lofty or worthy their motives. If peace is to exist at all on this planet it must first be created in the human heart, and the national interest of Canada demands that all our efforts be directed toward this primary objective.

First, Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the compliments which have been paid to the mover and seconder of the speech from the throne. I think they did a very creditable job in discharging this very important duty.
The settlement of the railway strike is, I think, something that should give us all a reason for feeling very happy. A terrific mental and economic strain has been lifted from the minds of the people of Canada, not only those who were directly connected with the strike but also those communities which were the innocent victims of its effects. I am sure that with this return to normality they will all be breathing more easily.
With regard to the speech from the throne itself I think that we as ordinary members look to it in anticipation of finding something there that will be beneficial, first of all, to the public of Canada as a whole. Then, I suppose, in a more selfish manner we look at it to see whether it presents some ray of hope for those in our constituencies whose welfare we have the responsibility of safeguarding. As one of the members from an agricultural area I regret I can see nothing in the speech from the throne which throws out any fresh ray of hope to the people whom I represent. As usual, of course, the farmer is caught in the cost-price squeeze; he must sell everything on an uncontrolled market and buy everything back on a controlled
The Address-Mr. Yuill market. From what I see in the speech from the throne there is not the slightest indication that this government is even remotely interested in trying to do anything for the farmer. Because of the huge surplus of grain and the inability of this government to sell it, the farmers have had to seek alternative means of bolstering up their economy. They have had to diversify their efforts by trying to raise cattle or hogs or poultry; or they have been producing eggs as a means of supplementing their revenue and seeking some reasonable equation between the ever increasing cost of production and the revenue that accrues from their untiring efforts.
Let us consider, for example, the problem with regard to egg production and the instability of the prices that prevail by examining the poultry products market report of August 31, 1956, and, again, the report for November 16. We find that the major marketing centres such as Vancouver, Calgary, Regina, Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal show a most marked variation in price between August 28 and November 16. On the earlier date the average price for "A" Qarge) eggs in those centres was 53 cents a dozen, and in a matter of about ten weeks-or on November 16-it was 36 cents a dozen, a difference of 17 cents a dozen.
Again, taking the report of August 28, we find the pricespread to the producer between "A" (large) and "A" (medium) eggs in the markets quoted varied from four cents in Calgary to 17 cents in Toronto. Similarly, the spread between "A" (medium) and grade "B" varied from two cents a dozen at Montreal to 20 cents at Calgary.
I think that such glaring differences in price between the various marketing centres is not very indicative of an orderly marketing system and I believe the government could very well do something to help stabilize these prices. I do suggest that the 38 cents "floor price" on grade "A" (large) eggs should be given to the producer, not to the wholesaler. I think it should be a guarantee to the producer that that will be his minimum sale price for grade "A" eggs. The wholesaler has a chance to get his own profit. He has the right to increase his price by 14 cents a dozen, which I think would give him a very good margin.
Again, taking the poultry business, in some areas of the country it is a very important industry and I would say particularly so in the case of sections of British Columbia. In the poultry business there has been perhaps the greatest drop in prices of any phase of the agricultural industry. To take my own community as a criterion, the price of turkeys was 20 cents a pound cheaper in 1956 than

The Address-Mr. Yuill in 1955. In 1955 grade A turkeys were bringing 53 cents a pound. In 1956 they were bringing 33 cents a pound. It is quite true that there was an increase in the production of turkeys and poultry in general but I think one depressing effect was the number of turkeys imported from the United States. I think that had a very depressing effect upon the normal markets of British Columbia particularly and in an indirect way it affected our own Alberta markets.
When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), as of February 1, 1955, saw fit to remove the subsidy of $5 a ton on feed wheat or feed in general shipped to the people of British Columbia I think he posed an economic problem there that has not been solved up to this time. From the viewpoint of the Canadian economy I believe the minister could very well be classified as being penny wise and pound foolish.
We in Alberta suffered the loss of a large part of the British Columbia market basically, I presume, because of little or no opposition to United States turkeys coming into British Columbia and again perhaps of the freight differential we lost very heavily so far as our normally good market in Vancouver is concerned.
Let us take another phase of this diversified industry and look at the situation with respect to hogs. According to the Livestock and Meat Trade Reports we find that the average price of hogs at four major marketing centres, Toronto, Winnipeg, Moose Jaw and Calgary, for the first nine months of 1955 was $23.06 a hundredweight. For the first nine months of 1956 the average price was $22.75 a hundredweight. Taking the five year average for the years 1951 to 1955 inclusive, we find that the price was $27.70 a hundredweight. This indicates considerable shrinking in hog prices in the last two years.
I think it is quite obvious that the floor price of $18.25 existing in Alberta today is not compatible with the cost of production and I believe it should be raised. There is one way that I believe the government could help the producer of hogs quite materially and at the same time it would have an overall desirable effect. I suggest that the government should double the bonuses paid on the top two grades of hogs.
Turning to the cattle industry, never in the history of Canada has there been more production of beef than in 1956. In spite of that we are becoming a net importer of beef. In my opinion there are two reasons for that. First, there is the natural and rapid growth of the country. Coupled with that is the fact that on a per capita basis we are becoming greater eaters of beef.


One would imagine that because we are producing more and the demand is greater the price of beef would strengthen as a consequence, but I do not think that holds true. If you look at the Livestock and Meat Trade Reports you will see that the average price of good steers at Toronto for the first ten months of 1956 was $19.32 a hundredweight and $18.25 at Winnipeg. From the Livestock Market Review we find that the average price at Toronto for the years 1951 to 1955 inclusive was $24.40 and $23.19 at Winnipeg. This indicates quite a substantial difference. The high price in 1956 was reached in August and then the price started to recede. Prices went down and down until the end of the year.
There are one or two suggestions I might make that I think would be beneficial and in the interests of everyone concerned, not only the producer but the consumer as well. I believe the time has come when beef should be sold according to its true value. I believe it would be in the interests of everyone concerned for beef to be rail graded in the same way as pork. There are so many cases where the producer brings an animal to the packing plant or stock yard and the buyer of the "critter", particularly if it is an off type, must play it safe. He may be buying the animal for a packing plant or somebody else. But as a consequence he always tips the grade balance in favour of himself or the person for whom he is buying with the result that the producer is unduly penalized.
I do not think you can blame anybody particularly. It may be regarded perhaps as the normal course of good business but I am sure that the packing plant together with everybody else is interested in seeing that the producer gets a fair price for his commodity. I strongly urge the government to give serious consideration to bring about what seems to me to be a most equitable method of selling the farmer's commodity so as to arrive at a realistic basis where the farmer will receive value for the produce he delivers.
There are many things I should like to speak about. I think that my colleague, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), has made it very clear where we stand on the question of pensions, and there should be no doubt in anybody's mind about our position. The other day my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Holowach), was discussing certain problems of the municipalities and asked what the government was going to do. There was an interjection from across the floor by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) who asked what Alberta was doing. I know, and everyone

else knows that had my colleague from Edmonton yesterday had time he could have answered that quite realistically. But because of the time element he was not in a position to answer. As one who has been associated with school administration for 25 years and as mayor of Barrhead for almost 12 years, I think that perhaps I am qualified to answer on behalf of my colleague from Edmonton East. I have here, I would imagine, around 180 statements which deal specifically with the amounts of grants, direct and indirect broken down to show how these grants affected the economy of these municipal districts by village, town, city, rural municipality or county.
If the hon. gentleman asked his question in sincerity I believe I can give him an answer which would give him at least some reasonable peace of mind. I have heard him interject so often that I find it very hard to accept that his is an honest question. For his benefit, and the benefit of the others who seem to have lost their sense of balance to quite a degree, I would like to give you a few figures. I have here, as I said before, records based on 1955 performance. Before closing my remarks I would like to deal with another matter which some of my colleagues have raised, that is with the increase in family allowances and old age pensions. Mr. Speaker, I may seem a little tardy, but I believe it is my duty to say a few words in connection with the speech from the throne.
I would like first to congratulate the honourable member for Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Hanna) for the brilliant and tactful manner in which he accomplished the delicate task of moving the address in reply. I am also very happy indeed to voice my appreciation to the honourable member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) who has so ably seconded the mover.
The speech from the throne reveals that, on the whole, Canada is enjoying a very high level of prosperity. As a matter of fact, it would be enough to travel abroad, to visit other countries, to find out how privileged we are to live in Canada and where the people enjoy so much affluence and freedom. Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the members of the opposition that such conditions are due to the good administration of the Liberal government. I would like to tell them how privileged we are in

Canada to have as leaders men of such ability, of such skill to administer and develop this country. These men have given proof of their skill at the United Nations, at NATO, in the meetings at Geneva, New Delhi, etc., as well as during the negotiation of trade treaties, and that is why the voice of Canada is one of the most respected in the world.
While reading a few paragraphs from the report of the Gordon commission, I noted the forecast that the population of Canada will probably double within 25 years. Of course that depends on the development of this country, and if there is one area which should be developed and settled it is my constituency of Chapleau with all its great farm lands and natural resources.
First of all, the federal and provincial governments will have to agree on building roads and railways there; if, for instance, a road was built branching off the present Canadian National line, from a point between Senneterre and La Reine, and as far as James bay, that is a stretch of about 225 miles, it would be possible to open up the northwestern part of Quebec, and establish there several parishes, because the soil is very fertile, and this would only facilitate the development of mines, hydro power, and forest resources. To further this northern expansion, a new railway trunk would have to be built which would branch off the new line now being built towards Chibougamau close to Cedar Rapid or Beattyville, as far as Matagami lake, a run of about 50 miles. This would give companies a chance to erect a paper mill which would help develop this new country covered with beautiful forests, and filled with minerals of all kinds. That is the type of development this country needs to increase its population and supply it with employment. This is so true that, although the construction of the railway from Barraute to Chibougamau has not yet been completed the population has already substantially increased. New parishes are already being established, those for instance at Bachelor lake, Opemiska, and there is even talk of others being founded north of Chibougamau.
Moreover, the federal and provincial governments should get together to help the federated co-operative build a slaughter house and a cold-storage, and also to help the companies that would like to build refineries and paper mills. My observations are based on statistics and on past experience because, when I came to Abitibi, there was only a handful of families, and there are now there at least 250,000 people.
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to miss this opportunity to repeat, in connection with our national security, that a road should be opened between Norembega, in the province
The Address-Mr. D. Gourd of Ontario, and the town of La Reine in the province of Quebec, a distance of only 47 miles. It is inconceivable that the Ontario government should overlook the necessity of building that road which, besides being beneficial to the province, would open the way to the settlement of many new parishes and provide a link between the two provinces, and promote the tourist trade in northwestern Quebec and northern Ontario. I could mention another road section whose development, by the Department of National Defence, would unquestionably be both necessary and urgent. I refer to the construction of a road connecting Casey, where the National Defence department has built a very important airport, to the radar station of Parent, a distance of about 25 miles. The cost of construction would certainly not exceed $12,000 to $15,000 per mile and the population of Parent and the surrounding district would thus be provided with an outlet.
I wish also to take this opportunity to ask our devoted Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to urge the government to grant the old age pension without the means test from the age of 65. This would spare us heavy administrative expenses and would be fairer to the people concerned. I would also like to ask him to increase family allowances. I can tell you that they are most useful in helping the families of my constituency in sending their children to school and in facing the rising cost of living. It would only be fair and reasonable to increase the rate of allowances. It would also be fair and proper to increase disabled persons' pension.
Mr. Speaker, you will no doubt pardon my obstinacy in again referring to the necessity for our country to be represented in the Vatican state along with almost every country in the world. It is with pleasure that I find myself in agreement with certain hon. members who understand that Canada is important enough to all points of view to have its own ambassador and not have to be represented by other countries, as it is the case now. To my mind it would be easy to arrive at an agreement in this matter and it would be in the interest of this country as a whole.
I would not want to conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, without mentioning, as I did in my previous speeches, the need for a distinctive Canadian flag. I support the suggestion made by the hon. member from Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier) that the leaders of all parties in the house come to an agreement on the choice of that flag. I am sure that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in discussing this matter with party leaders, will

The Address-Mr. Knight find with them a practical and just solution, which will be a credit to our great country, Canada.

Mr. Speaker, may I first endorse the words of congratulations that my leader conveyed to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the motion in reply.
In looking over the domestic scene I think one must agree that the greatest problem with which we are faced is this problem of inflation, and I would couple with it the related problem of the economic farm crisis in Canada. That has a good deal of importance to the people in the prairie west from which I come. It is sometimes called the farm cost-price squeeze.
I do not propose here to discuss the causes of inflation; that would serve no particular purpose. However, I do wish to plead the case of some of those who have been and who are affected by it. I shall also say a word or two about the only prescription for that particular disease with which the government has come forward, and it is indeed more than a prescription because the medicine itself has been forced upon us. I mean, of course, the manipulation of the interest rates upwards. Admittedly there has been a great expansion and great productivity. No one can shut his eyes to that. However, there are those who would sum up those two terms in the single word prosperity; with that I would take issue because surely there must be in the meaning of that word "prosperity" some element of general human happiness and contentment, and there must be some trickling down through the economic strata, all the strata of society, some benefit from our natural production, some equity if you like, in the sharing of the wealth which people produce. A real prosperity, as I say, would entail the sharing of some of this so-called prosperity by everyone in the country. But if this is prosperity it is an uneven prosperity. This government has no machinery, as far as I can see here, for a solution of this problem. It appears as hopeless in the face of inflation
(Mr. Gourd (Chapleau).]

as its twin the last Conservative government appeared in the face of deflation, inflation and deflation being two sides of the same coin.
When I said that the government was helpless in bringing forward a solution, perhaps I gave the government too much credit. Wealth is being syphoned off, of course, by vested interests, and indeed the government may justly be said to be aiding and abetting that particular process. And by what devices? There are many that I would mention but those which come to my mind readily are things like accelerated depreciation, depletion allowances, or by allowing the 20 per cent deduction from the income taxes in respect of the amounts of their profit from corporation dividends. That I have always thought to be particularly unjust. I know the motive behind it but I think it is time it was removed. Then there is the other one which usually irritates me; that is the ceiling on the contribution to the old age pension fund. Those who have a high income and reach the ceiling pay no more towards the old age pension part of the income tax than those who are on very modest income.
I do not think that prosperity is the word for this whirlwind of borrowing and spending in which we are all caught up, and which does leave a good deal of wreckage in its path. I have thought of the effects of inflation upon the farmer. The farmer is the forgotten man, I think, in Canada; at least that is the way we feel about it in western Canada. Not only has there been a steady decline over the years in the price of his produce, but there has been a corresponding, and perhaps even faster, rise in the cost of production and the cost of the machinery which he uses. The agricultural industry is declining. There is no doubt about it and I think it is a misfortune. I do not know whether we are prepared to go into the tinsel and glittering atomic age with almost complete urban living. It is a good thing to have good sound people on good sound and prosperous family farms. I am a city member, of course, but I am well aware of the extent to which the prosperity of the city and town is bound up with the prosperity of the farmers who surround that particular city or town.
It occurs to me to say that Mr. Walker, who is the secretary of the retail merchants association, said in the year end statement not too long ago that 250 small private businesses had disappeared through bankruptcy in Saskatchewan in the year 1956. Those were

private enterprise businesses, and my laissez faire friends across the way say it is just too bad but there is nothing that can be done about it. The prosperity of those people was predicated directly on the prosperity of the farmer. It also occurs to me to say what a howl of glee would have gone up on the part of my free enterprise friends if these had been publicly owned, perhaps Saskatchewan government owned projects, and in their opinion, would have been all the proof you need that you cannot have successful public enterprise. These were small private enterprises and as far as we in the C.C.F. are concerned we would have liked to have seen those little private enterprises continue to live and continue to be successful.
The result of inflation felt most in the average Canadian home is, of course, the cost of living. Someone told me the other day-I have no documentary proof of it-that one-third of the money value of the gross national product was due to the increase in prices. The rise in cost is followed, justly enough, by a demand for increased wages. We have, therefore, this spiral; up and up it goes and, if I may paraphrase a nursery rhyme, where it ends nobody knows. Those who suffer most are those who are on fixed incomes. When one thinks of the purchasing power of the dollar of an old age pension nowadays as compared to the same power at the time when the old age pension was initiated, one realizes that we have not come very far in the direction of giving security to our old people, because the purchasing power of the dollar has been destroyed. The value of people's life savings has been cut in half. Each one of us knows that, in regard to the life insurance we undertook in our early years, if we have to cash it in

and I say it is a sad commentary upon this so-called prosperity that many less fortunate people are cashing them in in order to provide themselves with the daily necessities of life-we only receive about half what we had some reason to expect. The same thing is true, of course, of government bonds. That forsooth is prosperity. If that is prosperity, may I repeat, it is a very uneven one.
In family allowances, of course, we hear the same thing. I am in favour of family allowances; I am a believer in old age pensions. We in this group have perhaps contributed something to the acquiring of these things. I shall not go into that. Then, there is the matter of hospital costs. Medical costs are going up and up so that-I was going to say for the average man but we will not put it that way

for the people below average in income the thing is getting to be almost
The Address-Mr. Knight impossible. It is true that in our own province and in other provinces there are hospital schemes that do relieve the situation.
I notice that even Liberal members are asking for an increase in the old age pension. I take hope. I think that may be a favourable omen because, if my hon. friends across the way will excuse me, I do not think they would be embarrassing their own government to such an extent by talking on old age pensions if they had not some pretty good idea that a rise in such pensions was coming. I do not know what amount will be forthcoming. However, I would urge upon the government that if my case is a good one, it be answered, and if this thing called prosperity is to be evened up for all strata of society, the government will be compelled in the very name of justice itself to bring forth an increased security program for old age pensioners, for the recipients of family allowances, for blind pensioners, for pensioners of all kinds, so that the augmented pension will have some resemblance in purchasing power to the pension when it was first given. Personally, I would like to see a real increase and if we can get at least those amounts restored to the original purchasing power it would at least be a step in the right direction.
I would urge upon the government with regard to what I have said about medical and hospital services that they proceed to initiate at least something of the scheme which they have been promising us ever since 1919. Well, I have perhaps said enough on that subject in the time at my disposal.
I would like to say something on the effects of the remedy for inflation proposed. Before I do that may I quote from a clipping that I hold in my hand, which contains a statement on the increased cost of living. Perhaps I might document it. This information was supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics. There is a comment on it in an editorial as follows;
More significantly, the index-
Of course, that is the index of living costs.
-rose 3.4 points from March 1 to October 1, recording increases in five of the intervening months. This sudden spurt upwards in the index is but another evidence of the inflationary pressures which now are bedevilling the Canadian economy more than at any time since the early Korean war period of 1950-51.
I was going on to say that I should like to mention some of the effects of the government remedy. There is some doubt in a great many minds as to whether the remedy is actually effective or, if it is effective at all, whether it is sufficiently extended. I am no economist. I notice that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) took the

"Past", I said. It was about

"No", this fellow said, "but it helps". My hon. friend the minister corrected our young colleague, the Conservative member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), for being so brash as to dare to bring to the attention of the government something in which his people are interested. Perhaps, in spite of my hon. friend's superior knowledge, as an expert on most issues, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris had the right conception of what the function of a member of parliament should be.
Well, to get back to my speech-there is no time for stories-I would like to mention how the effect of this government's cure, namely, the rise in interest rates, affects the ordinary people that I know. The first thing I have noticed is that it is driving more and more people into the clutches of the money lenders, since people are attempting to square up their debts at an exorbitant rate of interest. I have noticed an increase in instalment buying. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) probably knows the figure, but the last figure of consumer credit I had was $2,400 million, and that in a period of prosperity. May I ask, what kind of prosperity is that?
I was going to say a word or two to the Minister of Trade and Commerce about the statement of an expert in his particular field. I refer to a statement, I think it is the yearly annual statement of the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, Mr. Muir. He said this, as reported by the Montreal Gazette on January 11:
It would seem, therefore, to he at least open to doubt whether the present facilities and techniques


available to our monetary authorities are sufficiently wide in scope to deal with present-day problems of credit control. The classical weapon-upward movement of interest rates, largely through commercial banks-may by itself prove an impotent policy. It may be taking too positive a view of a distant scene, but it would at least appear that, in order to be fair and in order to achieve the best results, our monetary and credit control may have to embrace a wider area of our financial world than it now does.
There, I submit, is the evidence of the expert.
There are one or two other classes of people affected by this high rate of interest. The increasing of the interest rate does help to redistribute money. Well, it does transfer money from the pocket of the borrower, who has little money to spare, to the pockets of the lender, who has more. It adds to the difficulties of a man trying to finance the building of a house. Was it only today, or was it yesterday, that we had the interpretation by the Canadian Press of a statement made in this house by the Minister of Public Works? I hold the Canadian Press dispatch in my hand. It reads as follows:
The government may soon move to boost the interest rate ceiling under the National Housing Act to encourage a greater flow of mortgage money for house building, it was learned today.
The minister was questioned on that. I do not recall that he gave a satisfactory answer; but the possibility is those young people who are trying to establish a home-by the way, it is almost impossible to get money on a modest home basis

would perhaps be faced with the payment of six per cent as an interest rate. This high rate of interest cripples the small businessmen. The large corporations can get along and do their own financing because they use depreciation and various other methods. I am thinking particularly of the big retail stores which are actually turning themselves into finance companies because they find it much more profitable to sell on credit than for cash. Their real profits are derived from the finance side of their business. It is true that they are able to lower the price of goods somewhat and by this method they squeeze the smaller stores out of business. I should not be surprised if some of the 250 businesses that went bankrupt in the province of Saskatchewan did so as a result of being hurt by that particular thing.
Turning from the individual for a moment I would like to ask about interest rates. Here we have municipalities which even before the increase in interest rates were at their wit's end to obtain funds to keep their schools in operation and to extend sewer and water facilities, and they have been forced to borrow money. My own city of Saskatoon had to pay 5i per cent interest in

The Address-Mr. Knight
order to carry on in supplying essential services. There is no distinction, and you would not expect any, since private capital is involved, between the rate which is charged to people who are putting in luxury items and those who are concerned with essential services. Those involved with luxuries make more profit and are able to pay a higher interest rate and so they are able to obtain the money. This is something concerning which the government should take action, but of course the government will not do anything about it because it does not believe at all in economic planning.
I now wish to say a word or two about a matter that is very dear to the hearts of people in my particular part of the province. I am referring, of course, to the proposed, for that is all it is up to this moment, South Saskatchewan river development scheme. I was disappointed as I have been disappointed before by the adamant statement of the Prime Minister, which leads me to believe we will get no action concerning this project even in this election year. I shall be interested to hear my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when he mounts the hustings in the province of Saskatchewan. He has contradicted the Prime Minister on other occasions. I remember reading a report of an occasion when both my hon. friend and the Prime Minister appeared on a platform one evening in the city of Regina. The Prime Minister said quite honestly what he has repeated here in recent days that nothing would be done about the dam and five minutes afterwards the Minister of Agriculture addressing the same audience proceeded to offer some hope and encouragement to the assembly that the project would be built, and this was done in the presence of the Prime Minister himself. Judging from the statement made today I suspect the matter will not be trotted out even in this election year, unless it be by the Minister of Agriculture.
I want to draw to the attention of the house this report with which fault has already been found in several quarters. I refer to the preliminary report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, commonly called the Gordon report. There is a very adverse report there with respect to irrigation. On page 27 of the report the following appears:
We suggest that substantial irrigation projects, while desirable from the standpoint of local areas, could be harmful rather than helpful to farmers in the aggregate.
The first thing I want to point out is that the South Saskatchewan river scheme is not solely an irrigation development, for the question of power is involved. Even if the
statement on irrigation were correct, the scheme cannot be judged on the basis of benefit or practicability in regard to irrigation alone. The statement is most contradictory because previously in discussing agriculture at page 26 the report says:
Demand will continue to rise for foods which can be produced profitably within a more intensive pattern of land use than is presently practised in Canada. This will be true as farmers move toward more meat production and higher output of poultry and eggs.
The report also refers to some form of fodder rotation to assist us in changing from a purely wheat economy. Anyone who lives in my part of the country and in the district to the southwest knows very well there is no security for the prairie wheat farmer in switching to mixed farming in that particular area. As far as I am concerned, I believe irrigation is the means of bringing about the kind of security the report mentions, and more than that it would provide the increased population to consume some of the food which would result from the implementation of the recommendations in the report. The population would be further augmented by the attraction to the province of those industries which would naturally follow upon irrigation, proof of which can be found in the southern part of the province of Alberta where you have sugar refineries, canning plants and the beef finishing industry. There you have the ideal situation that can develop on a dry belt in the prairie provinces. My second appeal to the government is to pay no attention to this part of the report but to proceed with the irrigation scheme.
There is one other matter with which I should like to deal before I resume my seat and although it may be considered a small matter by some hon. members of this house it deeply concerns the people of my constituency. Not too long ago the town of Sutherland, a railroad town on the outskirts of Saskatoon, amalgamated with the larger city. Naturally we got busy to try to get mail delivery service for that new part of the city. Well, after long delays the matter got under way, surveys were made and certain conditions were laid down. We were told that the city would have to mark the streets and name them and that 90 per cent of the people would have to write in giving their names and addresses under the new set-up, and I am told this has now been accomplished. When I recently inquired about the matter I was told that although we had fulfilled those conditions 90 per cent of the people had not yet advised that they have receptacles set up to receive the mail when it is brought around. I must say, sir, I know many people in the larger city of Saskatoon that have not yet

The Address-Mr. Knight established receptacles. For the last 30 years I have been receiving my own mail in my milk box although perhaps I should not admit that in the presence of the Postmaster General (Mr. Lapointe). I think it is time to stop this dilly-dallying and shilly-shallying- they are both good words and they rhyme- and get on with the task so that when the weather is a little warmer the mail will be brought around. Most people lived in hope of having mail service established before the cold weather set in. Although it is hard for our good postmen to deliver in cold weather it is, after all, their work, and if the service were established it would mean only one man would go to the post office instead of the 30 or 40 who now have to go daily. Let us proceed with the matter and complete it. Surely it will have been completed before the election at least.
One other subject with which I want to deal is one of which I am particularly fond. I have noticed the measures granting aid to education that have been foreshadowed in the speech from the throne. We recognize that the rapid growth of our country requires a similar development of our universities and we approve without any reservation the financial participation of the state as long as the federal government does not intend to interfere in the field of education, . . .
Then we have that rhyme that we always have from some of my friends across the way. There is no one in this house who


is more insistent than I, that the administration and curriculum of education should be completely within provincial jurisdiction. Then he goes on further and refers to financial assistance as constituting another means of safeguarding our cultural economy. He then went on in praise of the government and said:
It recognizes the increased demands brought about by our national evolution. It therefore proposes to revise once more and to increase subsidies and subventions to provincial governments to assist them in providing technical and vocational training for our young people.
So the hon. member is in complete accord with grants to universities; he is in complete accord with grants to technical schools; he is in complete accord with grants for technical training. No matter what precautions we try to take to avoid it being done there will be some who would affirm, if you were going to do something about municipal government, that we were aiming at destroying the Catholic religion and the French language in the province of Quebec. Could anything be more silly, more groundless than that?
I hope I shall live long enough, and I hope the Prime Minister will too, to see the day when he will be willing and will dare to say that the idea that financial aid to the provinces for the purpose of education would ipso facto mean federal control over education is also silly. My time is about up but I have one concluding sentence. If it is a personal one I hope you will forgive me. Surely there is no man in this house, I do not care what his racial origin or religion may be, who can say that I have been anything but sincere in my belief that if we grant the provinces sufficient funds that there can be across this country not equal education but equal opportunity for education. It is all right for some of the provinces. I take it the province of Ontario can finance its own education. I am pleased to see that the premier of Quebec has given large sums to the support of education in his own province. But nobody who comes from the province of New Brunswick or the province of Nova Scotia, for instance, would say that those provinces can afford to give their children an equal opportunity for education such as can be given by some of the richer

Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few comments in this debate may I first of all be allowed to offer my sincere appreciation to the Prime Minister for his happy and tactful choice of the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In asking a representative from the western prairies in the person of the genial Irish Canadian from Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna), and the lively and active young member for Gloucester in the maritimes (Mr. Robichaud), to undertake this important parliamentary duty, the Prime Minister has once again demonstrated his broad and deep concern, and recognition of, the fact that Canadians are one family. He has again underlined by this generous gesture the necessity of unity for the future happiness and prosperity of the Canadian people. Allow me to offer my best wishes and congratulations to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona and the hon. member for Gloucester on the splendid performance of their duties.
Coming from Saskatchewan as I do, I wish also to congratulate the new leader of the official opposition. Though he was not born on the western prairies, as I was, nevertheless, like our politically and physically indestructible Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), he came to Saskatchewan at an early age and has given all his life and all his talents to that great province. I may also add another word. There are some members in this house who have been honoured by the red man of this country by being made Indian chiefs. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and I have both had this honour conferred upon us, and so have some other members of this house. Thus, in addition to my political congratulations, as one chief to another I offer him my good wishes.
