It is quite obvious, Mr. Speaker, that every speech from the throne must cover a variety of subjects and that any comment on it cannot help but follow much the same pattern. The speech from the throne is, as a rule, divided into three main parts. It

The Address-Mr. Mang covers the international scene; it deals secondly with the national picture and the progress of the economy of the nation as a whole; and, thirdly, it brings to light and deals with conditions in particular areas of Canada, attempting to fit the program of these particular areas into the Canadian scene as a whole.
In this present session, as has already been pointed out by other speakers, a great deal of emphasis is placed on the international scene. The reason for this is, I think, obvious. In this modern world no nation can long remain prosperous and happy by itself alone. Indeed, it is becoming increasingly evident that what other nations do, either politically or economically, affects the life and happiness of every Canadian citizen. Speaking as a prairie westerner, I need cite only one example to give one minor illustration. Between 70 and 80 per cent of our wheat must find an export market. In consequence of this the agricultural policies of all our 80 customer nations throughout the world will affect the marketing of our product, while the agricultural policies of our competitors such as the United States and Argentina, by their disposal and sales decisions, will also affect the life of every Canadian in western Canada.
Last year this parliament in its wisdom granted some $32 million to the farmers of western Canada in an attempt to assist them in their problem of storing the surplus crops which had been produced, and in making that grant every taxpayer in Canada was affected. We appreciate the assistance very much because it did mean something like seven cents a bushel to us. That is to us in the west another illustration of the effect that this interdependence of nations throughout the world economy can have for all of us. Not only what happens in the field of trade but events in the field of politics mean that our interest is bound up with the world interest and the interest of every other nation.
What happened, for instance, in Suez and Hungary recently has affected Canada as well as the rest of the world. Little did we dream last September that we would be host to thousands upon thousands of Hungarian refugees at the present time. While I am drawing attention to this phase of international developments in recent weeks and months, and while I am mentioning the refugee Hungarians, I would just like to say that I saw some of the work done by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) in bringing some of these refugees over to this country. That was shortly before I left to attend this session.


The first arrival of Hungarian refugees at Regina was the occasion of a very warm reception. I was very interested in attending this occasion, on the evening of their arrival, because there is in my constituency of Qu'Appelle a large community of Hungarian people who went there at the turn of the century and who have since contributed much to the economy of that particular area as, indeed, they have contributed to that of other areas in Saskatchewan. I mention that to indicate that we should welcome these people from Hungary most wholeheartedly, as was done on that occasion. Many people from this community in my area were at the welcoming reception and took part through interpreters and also in a more tangible way, having gathered finances, in helping to establish these people in this country.
A further reason for mentioning this at this time is that I think it shows that Saskatchewan has taken to heart the words of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration just before he left for Europe when he admonished the communities of Canada to render every possible assistance in the placement and welcoming of these Hungarian patriots when they arrived here. Saskatchewan is doing this in a very commendable way.
There was one item on the agenda that evening that was most impressive. At one stage of the proceedings the chairman of the welcoming reception called upon the Hungarian patriots to rise and sing for us the Hungarian national anthem. By the time they had come to the second stanza of the anthem their emotions were very evident. Tears began to flow and at the end of their stirring rendition of the anthem the silence was such as to move all those present. We followed by singing God Save the Queen, and looking at the faces of these new Canadians I could see a spirit that will, I am sure, contribute a great deal to the progress of Canada, and when the time arrives for them to become Canadians I am sure they will make a great contribution to our national life.
I spoke to many of these people. They were from all classes of society. I spoke to engineers, mechanics, labourers, tailors, farmers and housewives. It seemed that a cross-section of the people of Hungary had been brought to our country and would be of great benefit to us. I noted in the paper today that of all the hundreds who have come here there are only about 35 who have not yet been placed in employment.
May I say a word or two about the recent railway strike that affected my constituency as I am sure it did every other constituency

in Canada. For the past few years we have been very anxious to get our products off the farms into a saleable position. In our particular area we have a good many shipping points where some millions of bushels of grain are produced. Before I came here for this session I had telephone calls and interviews with people who urged me to do what I could to bring to bear the sentiments of the farmers of Qu'Appelle constituency in order that the strike might be settled speedily.
I think that the government and particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) are to be congratulated on the manner in which this unfortunate and expensive interruption in the nation's economic life was dealt with. It is not easy for a third party to step in and intervene in the affairs of two stubborn disputants. Everyone will agree that it would have been a very unhappy situation if parliament had been forced to intervene in the matter. Even if it had become necessary to settle the strike and interruption of railway service through legislative action by using the machinery of parliament and introducing the element of compulsion, I do not think that the resumption of service could have been achieved more quickly and certainly not as satisfactorily.
As all of us know, parliament met on Tuesday and by Friday afternoon a solution to the deadlock was announced. Legislative action would have brought about ill will as well as throwing the matter into politics, which was to be avoided at all costs. Such a course would have caused confusion of the issues, confusion of the public mind and would have given birth to recrimination and disunity among Canadians.
Once again the Prime Minister has proven his ability to put immediate issues in their proper perspective and arrive at a reasonable solution. To solve the difficulty in this way and to have the ability to bring about a compromise in such a manner is nothing short of genius on the part of any individual. When the Prime Minister was created an honorary chief of the Great Plains Indians at Fort Qu'Appelle some years ago, an event at which I was happy to attend, he was named wise counsellor. I submit to hon. members that no Canadian deserves that title more or carries it with greater dignity.
Perhaps this may afford me an opportunity to say a few words with respect to the attitude of farmers and consumers in general. With regard to economic dislocations caused by disputes between corporations and labour organizations in the modern economic set-up in the world and in this country, I think we have come to the point where we must take
The Address-Mr. Mang a very hard look at the justification for break-downs such as strikes cause. In our highly organized society of today, whether in this country or any other, if one group however small-and this was illustrated by the recent strike-uses the power of its organization in order to attain its ends in a way that does not always indicate the highest sense of social responsibility, shall I say, I believe it will bring about a reaction on the part of those sections of society which are not as powerfully organized as the corporations or the labour unions. Because of the very nature of his occupation and also because of his temperament, the farmer is not in a position to organize and assert his economic strength. On account of the very nature of the way in which farmers earn their living and the very nature of the temperament of the individual farmer, it is not possible for them to marshal their economic strength and bring themselves to the point of economic welfare in the way that other sections of the community can.
The consumer is in much the same position. By the very nature of the consumer population in any country they cannot be organized to assert their economic rights and negotiate by means of ultimatum. Corporations can negotiate, and do very often bring negotiations to the point where they can issue an ultimatum and say either you come to terms with us as a corporation or we will close down and throw you out of employment. On the other hand, powerful labour organizations can also issue ultimatums and say, unless you meet our conditions and our demands we will not conform to an agreement. Now, that is nothing short of a shooting war in the economy of a nation. That attitude, I think, is in time going to bring about a reaction with which the public is going to deal in a way which is not desirable in a democracy.

The surplus of wheat in Canada at present does not seem to have arisen out of the procedures used to market the crop. It has resulted primarily from weather conditions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join the previous speakers who have taken part in this throne speech debate in extending my congratulations to the mover, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna), and the seconder, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), on the fine contribution they have made and the manner in which they discharged their responsibilities in this debate. However, I cannot with the same enthusiasm extend congratulations to the authors of the throne speech, because I have come to the conclusion that many problems affecting the people of Canada have not been considered or dealt with in the presentation of the speech.
I do, however, wish to say that the grants to municipalities, which the government proposes to pay in lieu of taxes for federal property and buildings located within the boundaries of municipalities, and which require necessary municipal services, is a most welcome aspect of the throne speech. If we are to assume that the intention of the government is to pay grants in lieu of taxes on the normal assessment of any particular municipality, it would mean that the property located in the city of Oshawa, as an example, would annually bring an additional $40,000 in revenue to that municipality.
This matter has been continually advocated by members from this side of the house for many years and proposals have been submitted to the government in this respect. I, personally, have brought this matter to the attention of the government on a number of occasions. Unfortunately these proposals are either rejected at once or are heard in stony silence by the government. Instead of taking immediate action on sound proposals such as this, this government has a tendency to postpone action for four or five years. In my opinion, financial matters in respect to municipalities are not matters to be delayed but rather are of sufficient importance to be acted upon immediately.
The approximately 4,000 municipalities in Canada have had difficulties in raising money for necesary services and capital expenditures for quite some time. This pressure on the municipalities is getting more acute year by year. We are told that Canada leads the world in industrial expansion; that Canada is booming. We are also told that our productive capacity, our national income and our output of goods are rising to dizzy heights undreamed of even a decade ago. But for
The Address-Mr. Starr what reason do we work, save and invest, except to raise our family and individual standard of good living? These are the very things we expect our municipalities to provide-hospitals, schools, community services and comfortable, well-protected homes, well supplied with power, water and sewage systems in keeping with a progressive civilization.
But what is the situation today? The fact is that we are lagging behind in all these things. We are not getting the benefits of this boom because our municipal governments are being denied a fair share of the Canadian tax dollar. This situation is the result of the federal government's policy of monopolizing the major share of the tax dollars raised by all governments. The federal government is most reluctant to relinquish some of the taxing powers that were enjoyed previously by the provinces and the municipalities. This question of taxing power is most unfair and unjust. The result is that a heavy burden has been placed on the small home owner in the Dominion of Canada.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, the federal government is loath to part with even a slight portion of their share of the tax dollar in order to relieve the small home owner, but seems rather to enjoy and jealously hoard this taxing power within its scope. There is no question as to the heavy real estate tax burden that is now being borne by the small home owner of every municipality in order to pay for the many services that municipal councils are called upon to supply. The municipalities of all our provinces face the same problems. It does not really matter by what name we call them, whether it be townships, cities, towns or villages. In the long run they are all part of a level of government which is just as essential to the federal principle as are the provinces or the government of Canada. It would be a real catastrophe if a time should come when they are forced into obscurity or insignificance by any other level of government. This seems to me to be the real danger of the centralization of so many functions and powers of government here in Ottawa. It would also be a calamity if the municipalities were forced by sheer necessity of every day problems to so increase the tax load that home owning becomes in Canada a mark either of great wealth or of economic folly.
I wish to remind this house that no less than 80 per cent of municipal taxation is borne by real estate. According to the latest figures issued by the dominion bureau of statistics we find that in 1939 the tax dollar was shared as follows:	The federal

The Address-Mr. Starr government received 48 cents; the provincial government, 22.3 cents; and the municipal government 29.7 cents. At the present time the federal government has increased its share to 77 cents of the tax dollar; the provincial government has been reduced to 12 cents; and the poor cousin of the senior governments, the municipality, receives 11 cents.
The Canadian tax dollar represents the total amount of all tax collections at the levels of the three authorities which under our Canadian federal system have the responsibility in the matter of the expenditure of public funds. In the past number of years the federal government has encroached upon the Canadian tax dollar to an extent never before envisaged. I may be asked what the federal government should do immediately and constructively to help to meet this critical situation but I do not have to go far to find an answer.
In the first place there must be a rebalancing of the taxation powers between the federal government on the one hand and the provinces and the municipalities on the other. In other words, the central government must learn, in the same way that we all must learn in our private lives, to get along on less. Taxation must be reduced, particularly the federal share of the Canadian tax dollar which must be brought within reason to allow the municipalities to levy taxes which are at least close to being in keeping with the increased demands on their resources.
We must remember that there is only so much money in the budget and if one member of a family takes more than he needs the others must suffer. I do not advocate that we all should share equally, but it does seem to me to make sense that each should participate in the family finances, not according to his strength, size or power but according to his needs as agreed upon in family council.
Since world war II municipalities everywhere have experienced a tremendous growth in population. They have experienced expansion in every phase of community life. The result has been that they have been burdened by the problem of raising funds to supply the various necessary services which include such important things as schools, waterworks, sewers and water mains. For these very necessary services the municipalities must sell debentures in order to raise capital. They try to do this at as low a rate of interest as possible.
The present bond market situation poses some very serious problems for municipalities which are obliged to raise increasingly large sums of money by debenture financing. Interest rates which have risen sharply in

the past 18 months reflect the general scarcity of funds for investment purposes. The prospects of a downward trend, while unpredictable even within the near future, do not appear evident for some time to come, and especially as long as present economic conditions continue.
This situation appears to have developed as a result of the substantially high level of capital investment that has been and is being experienced in Canada within recent years at least, which has brought into play competing forces for the available supply of funds both in this area and in the general area of consumer demands.
With a view to easing this situation the monetary authorities, through various means at their disposal, have made it increasingly difficult to borrow money through the medium of forcing upward adjustment of interest rates.
This action has been taken undoubtedly in the interests of the economy of the country as a whole and it is inevitable under such circumstances that some groups or segments of the economy are affected more seriously than others. Municipalities are in this category.
Municipalities at the present time have to compete for borrowings against other securities which suffer less from the impact of a monetary condition of this kind such as private corporations which are able to offer securities at high interest rates because the net cost after taxation is only about half of the actual interest paid.
In addition they are able to offer other inducements to potential investors such as through dividend participation, stocks, warrants, etc. The unfortunate effect of this on municipalities at least is that under present market conditions they are obliged to pay a higher rate of interest on their borrowings than their actual credit warrants.
Quite recently, as reported in the Oshawa Times-Gazette of Friday, January 11, 1957, over which the headline read "Tight money policy hits city finances", a meeting was held of the Oshawa city council in conjunction with the public utilities commission and the board of education of that city. It was reported that a debenture issue in the amount of $1,600,000 will be placed on the market within the next week and a close watch will be maintained in the bond market for an opportunity to market a further issue to cover the expenditure already made. This meeting was called at the request of the board of education to discuss the financing difficulties confronting the board of education and the public utilities commission building programs. It was pointed out that

an immediate addition to the water works would have to be made and that water supply problems were at a critical point during the summer of 1956 and only the unusually cool season prevented major water shortages.
The board of education is faced with a program of five new schools and they advised this meeting that $1,250,000 is needed immediately for one secondary and one elementary school which are being planned for this year. What interest rate will have to be paid in the present competitive market it is hard to say, but there is no doubt that it will be high and difficulty may be experienced in the sale of these bonds.
The most disturbing feature of the whole situation is that the investment market does not appear to make any particular distinction between municipal and other corporate borrowers. Everything must be competitive. Because of that, the very interests which cried the loudest when muncipalities got into trouble through excessive borrowings and high interest rates in the thirties are now contributing to what might conceivably develop into a similar situation again in some areas at least. In any event they are not doing anything to alleviate the situation. The question is what, if anything, can or should the municipalities do about the situation.
The unfortunate part is that many services of municipal governments cannot be postponed, even with the best will and intentions of the authorities concerned. Children cannot go without schools nor can people exist without the basic amenities of life, such as sewer and water mains. The result of the present situation means that the 4,000-odd municipalities in Canada will have to pay additional millions of dollars in increased rates of interest to supply these necessary services, which in turn will be an additional burden on the small home owner in the municipality.
It has been suggested time and time again to this government by these hard-pressed municipalities which I have mentioned that the federal government establish a fund from which municipalities could borrow money at a low rate of interest in order to institute these necessary programs. I urge the government, Mr. Speaker, to give this matter very serious consideration without any postponement. The time has come for immediate and decisive action in order to help these hard-pressed municipalities. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is an acknowledged principle of our way of life that the strong must help the weak and that the rich must assist the poor. If these principles are adhered to I am sure that a great deal of the difficulty
The Address-Mr. Starr which now presents itself to the basic governments in our country could be alleviated.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the automobile excise tax for a few moments.
Although I have referred to the excise tax on automobiles in a number of previous speeches I have made in this house, and have also asked questions on the orders of the day, I feel it is necessary for me to bring this matter again to the attention of parliament.
This tax has readily been acknowledged by everyone as an unnecessary tax ever since it was instituted as a luxury tax, and at the present time it is most unsound. The automobile is now a basic necessity. At the present time a person buying an automobile pays $165 luxury tax when the automobile costs $2,500, though in the majority of cases the car is purchased for the purpose of driving to work. Also included in this price is another $165 in sales tax. To more than eight people out of ten a car is an absolute necessity.
To quote from a speech made by William A. Wecker, President of the Canadian Automobile Chamber of Commerce and President and General Manager of General Motors of Canada Limited, on August 28, 1956:
The history of our industrial development will record that much credit for our great progress in recent years is due to the automotive industry and the transportation provided by motor cars and trucks. Without them our economic life would remain narrow and restricted. It is unfair to tax as a luxury an item that makes such a contribution to our economy.
At the same time this discriminatory tax has a disruptive effect on our industry's efforts to provide an increasing measure of employment stability.
Two years ago, Mr. Speaker, I pointed out in this house that the loss of revenue from the decrease of the excise tax would not be very much, if any. I am sure that after the tax was cut by five per cent two years ago it was found that the additional revenue from the 10 per cent sales tax and the increased number of people employed who were eligible for income tax has more than made up the loss of revenue from the five per cent cut in excise tax.
The same thing would apply at the present time, and I urge the minister to give this matter his most earnest consideration. During the year 1955 the purchasers of new cars and trucks paid $172,189,762 in sales and excise tax.
Another very important matter in this connection is the application of tax reduction or removal on cars in the hands of dealers. At the present time the sales and excise taxes on passenger cars are collected by the manufacturer before the car goes to the dealer

The Address-Mr. J. R. Kirk for sale to the customer. This method is most unfair to all, and in effect treats these cars still in the salesroom and waiting to be sold as though they had actually been sold while the higher tax levels were in effect.
I bring this matter once again to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and hope that because of the representations which have been made by the automobile dealers in Canada he will give it his serious consideration and remedy this most unfair method of collecting taxes on automobiles.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to join with previous speakers in extending felicitations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I congratulate them upon the excellence of their material, and at the same time I must confess to envying them both a little for the ease with which they expressed themselves.
It is not my intention to delay the house with extensive comments on the various items of legislation mentioned in the speech from the throne. However, I do wish to make some brief references to matters of special interest to those in the constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough which I have been privileged to represent in this house since 1936. I hope that I can make up by sincerity of purpose for what I may lack in oratory.
Antigonish and Guysborough counties have one very definite thing in common-both have very long stretches of seacoast, and in both counties many of our residents depend for their livelihood upon the products of the sea. The first part fo my remarks will therefore deal with those things which affect our fishermen and the fishing industry generally.
First of all, may I compliment our able Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) for putting into effect, recently, legislation benefiting our fishermen. I refer to the insurance coverage for fishing boats, nets, traps and other fishing equipment which has already been of great assistance to the fishermen; also to the more recent step of extending unemployment insurance benefits to our fishermen.
In speaking in this house on March 16, 1953, I stressed, along with other matters, the need for insurance for fishermen against storm losses, and unemployment insurance coverage for farmers and fishermen. It is gratifying to note that for our fishermen at any rate these protections have now become a reality. Perhaps at a later date our farmers will also be brought under the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
At this point I am also going to reiterate other suggestions which I made on March 16, 1953, and in fact, as far back as 1948. These

have to do with a search and rescue service and improved aids to navigation. True, some steps have been taken by our capable Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) in connection with the first named, by the establishing of a helicopter-equipped service. This, of course, will take several years to bring to completion, but it is certainly a step in the right direction.
I hope that we will soon see this type of service put into operation along the maritime coast. In my constituency within recent months a tragedy occurred off the coast of Canso, resulting in the loss of several lives, which could conceivably have been averted if a more up-to-date coast-guard service had been available.
The second item of improved aids to navigation is something about which I feel very deeply. I appreciate what our fishermen go through as they leave their home ports during the fall and winter months long before daylight for the fishing grounds. Their return trip is plagued only too often with fog, rain, snow, sleet, along with nightfall, and they must often pin their hopes for a safe arrival upon the navigational aids provided by the Department of Transport. In my opinion these aids are often too sparsely distributed and of a kind not best suited to the fishermen's need.
Quite frequently in this regard the judgment of departmental officials overweighs that of the fishermen who from bitter practical experience are in a better position to know what types of aids will prove most advantageous. In making representations to departmental officials in this respect I find their stock reply, in some instances, is that the aid requested is not needed, though, to repeat, I believe the fishermen to be the best judges in the specific localities where they operate. Other replies are either that the materials for such aids are in short supply, or else that there are no funds available.
I do not want to be too hard on these departmental officials nor upon the government but, as I have said, I feel very strongly for our fishermen and I contend that more money could and should be made available to provide these necessary navigational aids.
The fishing industry on the Atlantic coast will be greatly heartened by the action of President Eisenhower in turning down the recommendation of the United States tariff board concerning the tariff on Canadian fish entering the New England market. I am sure this was not done without considerable interest being displayed by our Canadian government, and we in the east are grateful to all concerned.
At this point I might be permitted to refer, as previous speakers have done, to the

recently published preliminary report of the Gordon commission on the Canadian economy, and particularly to that part which deals with the Atlantic provinces. The commission indicates that there is much doubt whether anything can be done to improve the lot of the maritimers other than by helping them to buy one-way tickets to greener pastures in upper Canada. I have some suggestions as to what could be done to encourage our fishermen to remain at home and improve their earning capacity. What our fishermen lack, in my opinion, are certain facilities whereby they can increase their catch and steady markets where it can be disposed of at a reasonable price. By navigational aids such as I have already mentioned, by freight rate revisions and by expenditures on wharves, breakwaters and dredging our fishermen could increase their earning capacity and do so without too great a hardship.
In this connection I am going to bring to the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) some improvements which are very much needed in the fishing centres of Antigonish-Guysborough, improvements which would be more welcomed by our fishermen than any dole or transportation allowance such as the Gordon commission report suggests. Speaking offhand, I would list the following points where public works would be welcomed and are necessary:	Arisaig,
Malignant Cove, Livingstone Cove, South Lake, Morristown, Bayfield, Barrio's Beach, Cape Jack, Havre Boucher, St. Francis Harbour, Boylston, Peas Brook, Canso, Little Dover, Port Felix, Charles Cove, Larry's River, New Harbour, Drum Head, Isaac's Harbour, Liscomb, Marie Joseph and Ecum Secum.
All of these have been brought to the attention of the Department of Public Works at one time or another while I have had the honour to represent Antigonish-Guysborough, now nearly 21 years. Undoubtedly the increased activity which would develop in our fishing industry would be very considerable if public works would improve the facilities at these fishing points.
I should like to turn now to the farming industry of Nova Scotia. On December 13 last most of the Nova Scotia members of parliament met with representatives of the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture in Truro. This meeting was quite informal and the discussions covered a variety of subjects dealing with matters of most interest to our farming communities.
One thing stressed by the federation representatives was the need of what they referred to as a protection policy. They did not explain as fully as I would have liked just what
The Address-Mr. J. R. Kirk they had in mind, but I presume it refers to a stability which would result from a more reasonably balanced relationship between farm prices and farm costs. It is true that farmers, like other consumers, must buy many articles of daily living on a protected market while they must sell their products on an open market. I have no pretensions to being an authority on economics, agricultural or otherwise, but I should like to see something done to ease this imbalance experienced by our farmers. I may add that I am satisfied that if any government can thus bring added prosperity to our farming population this Liberal government can and will do it.
There are various measures which can assist, directly or indirectly, in providing better returns for our farmers and I should like to comment briefly upon some of them. I welcome the appointing of a Senate committee to review the problem of submarginal lands in eastern Canada. In my constituency, where most of our farms lie close to the sea, it is only to be expected that the land is not particularly fertile, especially so when one realizes that much of this land has been tilled for several hundred years. I believe that the results of this study will be truly helpful to our marginal farmers, directing their energies towards the best use and conservation of the land. I hope too that erosion problems, land drainage and reforestation will be included as topics for study by the committee.
Within the last year or two, community pasturage programs have been initiated in Nova Scotia and it is hoped that this will be further developed to the benefit of our cattle and sheep farmers.
One matter I wish to mention is the benefit to our farmers of the feed freight assistance policy initiated by this federal government.
I would urge that this policy be maintained and, indeed, be placed on a permanent basis.
With regard to freight rates, the situation today is that the Maritime Freight Rates Act is no longer helping maritime producers. Increases in freight rates have been so frequent in recent years that the time has come for a complete revision of the act if we are to enjoy any of the assistance envisioned by the act at its inception. I cannot emphasize too strongly to the government the need for such a revision and with the least possible delay.
The welfare of our farming communities is affected by the buying power of the people generally. When old age pensions and family allowances were first introduced by the Liberal government of prime minister Mackenzie King, the amounts decided upon were governed in great part by the purchasing power they represented, and certainly
384	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. J. R. Kirk during the years that have intervened this added purchasing power has been a boon to all phases of Canadian life. However, with the passing of years the purchasing power of the dollar has gradually dwindled, and nowhere is it more evident than in its application to these pensions. I believe I am correct in estimating that by far the greatest part of these pensions goes for increased 'ood costs, and to the degree that this is true at least I should like to see these pensions increased to restore to them the buying power which was originally intended.
It was good news to hear that federal grants to universities are to be increased and that vocational and technical schools will also profit from the government's recognition of the contribution being made by education to the development of Canada. I would express the hope, however, along with other hon. members, that the system of allocating the grants to universities will be changed to a more equitable basis as between province and province. The province of Nova Scotia now suffers in this respect from the fact that such a large percentage of its population endeavours to attend our halls of higher learning.
In my home town of Antigonish we have the university of St. Francis Xavier where many students come from other countries, attracted by the studies in co-operative methods and adult education in which our university has pioneered. We have, indeed, a miniature commonwealth of nations in our midst. Students from India, Pakistan, Bermuda, South America, the United States and even from far away Kenya colony come to St. Francis Xavier to join with our own Canadian students in the pursuit of knowledge. I know I speak for the governors of the university when I express to the Prime

Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) their thanks as well as my own for his warm interest in matters academic.
Upon reading the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, one cannot but be impressed by the remarkable strides forward that Canada has made both in economic expansion and in its position as a world nation during the past number of years under a far-sighted Liberal government. For our younger Canadians especially there are now no bounds to the avenues open to them, and who would dare to forecast the future that awaits them?
I should like to conclude these remarks with an excerpt from a speech made by former prime minister W. L. Mackenzie King, in Kingston on June 7, 1941, words which seem particularly applicable to Canadians of this era. He said:
In a country like Canada, every man is more or less the architect of his own fortune. Our great public men have become the architects of our country's future, without regard to birth or race or class. Intelligence, industry and integrity are the basic qualities by which they have achieved this goal, qualities to be had by any Canadian who has the will to persevere.
